For Jonathan and Rick and Christian Questions...

## Episode 732 — Got Armor?
Published: 2012-10-21
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/732-got-armor/

Romans 13:12: (NASB) The night is almost gone, and the day is near.

Therefore let us lay aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armor of light.

Last week we took a hard look at Islam and compared its message of devotion to that of Christianity. We looked at its personal and national approach to “jihad” and saw significant differences from our own Christian faith. Today we will focus on the Christian “jihad” – the Christian’s personal struggle to fight our warfare – not against others but against Satan. How do we fight this fight? What are we armed with? What makes us think such a battle against such an enemy can be won?

Who is the enemy and how do we secure our protection for this armed conflict?

Ephesians 6:10-12: (NASB) 10Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of His might. 11Put on the full armor of God, so that you will be able to stand firm against the schemes of the devil. 12For our struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the powers, against the world forces of this darkness, against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places.

Who is the enemy?

1 Peter 5:8: (NASB) Be of sober spirit, be on the alert. Your adversary, the devil, prowls around like a roaring lion, seeking someone to devour.

Rulers, powers, world forces of darkness, and spiritual wickedness are all headed by Satan himself! There is no bigger, badder, more brutal enemy that we could ever face! You had better be armed!

Ephesians 6:14: (NKJV) Stand therefore, having girded your waist with truth, having put on the breastplate of righteousness… Note the belt neither protects nor attacks, it simply holds everything together. (Source: Commentary by J. Vernon McGee, “Thru the Bible”) "Having your loins girt about with truth:" In the ancient garment of that day, the girdle about the loins held in place every other part of the uniform of the soldier. It was essential. To tell you the truth, if the girdle was lost, you lost everything.

Roman Legionary’s clothing (belt), Phalera Filmworks

- The military belt insures the weapons remained firmly in place. The belt is made of leather and has metal plates for both decoration and reinforcement. At the front is an apron of leather straps, decorated with metal disks and pendants.

John 17:17-18: (NKJV) 17Sanctify them by Your truth. Your word is truth. 18As You sent me into the world, I also have sent them into the world.

1 Peter 1:13-16: (NKJV) 13Therefore gird up the loins of your mind, be sober, and rest your hope fully upon the grace that is to be brought to you at the revelation of Jesus Christ; 14as obedient children, not conforming yourselves to the former lusts, as in your ignorance; 15but as He who called you is holy, you also be holy in all your conduct, 16because it is written, Be holy, for I am holy.

The truth of Scripture needs to be planted in and held firmly in our minds. It is profound that God’s word gives all of the rest of the armor a consistent base from which to be able to function.

Observations about this truth:

- It is of God – therefore of higher origin than any other source;
- It is consistent – it gives black and white principles from which we can deal with all shades of gray;
- It is eternal – it defines not only what has happened and what is at present, but it also defines what will be;
- It is irrefutable – it stands the tests of time, philosophy, compromise and doubt.

This truth is the foundation - perhaps the unnoticed foundation - for victory over Satan! That little belt of truth is very important in our Christian life. Just how good a weapon is the Shield of Faith?

Ephesians 6:16: (NASB) in addition to all, taking up the shield of faith with which you will be able to extinguish all the flaming arrows of the evil one.

What “style” shield is this? (Source: Bible Commentary from Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) Shield - the large, oblong, oval, door- like shield of the Romans, four feet long by two and a half feet broad; not the small, round buckler.

A buckler is a different kind of shield. Both types of shields are biblical:

Psalms 91:4: He shall cover thee with his feathers, and under his wings shalt thou trust: his truth shall be thy shield and buckler.

The buckler is a mobile protection, largely to be controlled by the soldier who bears it:

Proverbs 2:7: He layeth up sound wisdom for the righteous: he is a buckler to them that walk uprightly.

Observations about the shield:

- This shield is carried onto the battlefield – it can be put down.
- It is a massive portable protection – an offensive weapon for pushing back an enemy.
- It represents a double protection carried to cover the armor that one wears on the body.
- You won’t storm a castle with it! It’s meant to form a wall of defense.
- You will be protected when in a place of vulnerability – a place where there are no walls. It is a portable wall, just like our faith should be. Do we carry our portable wall wherever we go?
- This shield is specific to quenching the fiery darts of The Wicked One. A buckler would not suffice, as we are clearly overmatched in this battle. This type of shield is featured to send us a specific message: We are not to seek the hand-to-hand combat that would be appropriate for a buckler. We are to be on the battlefield with our fellow soldiers and fight together. There is safety within the fellowship of Christianity. As an example, in the early church, the Jewish Christians and the Gentile Christians had to learn to stand side-by-side and be willing to die together for their cause. The shield’s purpose is to protect our whole person. We need to be able to stay behind it to provide an added layer of protection from what could blindside us. We can’t fight the fight without faith.

Proverbs 18:10: The name of the LORD is a strong tower; the righteous runs into it and is safe.

When your shield is down in a position of difficulty, we can run to that strong tower!

Faith as a shield thwarting the darts of the enemy in action:

Psalms 56:1-4: (NKJV) 1Be merciful to me, O God, for man would swallow me up; Fighting all day he oppresses me. 2My enemies would hound me all day, for there are many who fight against me, O Most High. 3Whenever I am afraid, I will trust in You. 4In God (I will praise His word), in God I have put my trust; I will not fear. What can flesh do to me?

A caller suggested: Hebrews 11:6: Without faith, it is impossible to please God. Without faith, it is impossible to fight this battle against the wiles of the devil!

James 2:18-20: (NASB) 18But someone may well say, You have faith and I have works; show me your faith without the works, and I will show you my faith by my works. 19You believe that God is one. You do well; the demons also believe, and shudder. 20But are you willing to recognize, you foolish fellow, that faith without works is useless?

Faith with no works is like having the shield but staying home. We can’t cower in the background.

Works with no faith is like showing up on the battlefield with no shield. We can’t try standing on our own without God’s strength.

1 Peter 5:9: (NASB) But resist him, firm in your faith, knowing that the same experiences of suffering are being accomplished by your brethren who are in the world.

So, how do you use the Sword of the Spirit?

Ephesians 6:17: (NKJV) And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; All of the other armor is in place to protect and guard that which is vulnerable. This sword is the only purely offensive weapon, so what is it capable of doing?

2 Corinthians 5:17: (NKJV) Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation; old things have passed away; behold, all things have become new.

So, if the Spirit is described as a sword, we can safely say that this sword is a gift from God and it gives its chosen user a great power to wield.

It is called the “sword of the Spirit,” yet it is defined as the “word of God.” The new creation, begotten of the spirit of God, can use and understand the word of God. Anyone can use the word of God as a sword (such as a non-believer quoting a Scripture in a negative way), but not with the sword of the Spirit, using the attitude in which the Scriptures are presented. You need God’s Spirit to be able to properly use God’s word.

The Apostle Paul demonstrates some proper use of this power:

1 Corinthians 2:1-5: (NKJV) 1And I, brethren, when I came to you, did not come with excellence of speech or of wisdom declaring to you the testimony of God. 2For I determined not to know anything among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified. 3I was with you in weakness, in fear, and in much trembling. 4And my speech and my preaching were not with persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, 5that your faith should not be in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.

Observations about the sword:

- It is a weapon of offence we can use to attack the enemy.
- It is given to us to use in our hand.
- We choose how to wield it. Do we use it sparingly and only on Sundays, or every day?
- We can put it down.

Do you carry your sword in your phone?

What is a primary differences between all of the armor versus the Shield of Faith and the Sword of the

Spirit? All other armor is given by God and is fastened onto us. The Shield of Faith and the Sword of the Spirit, by contrast, are held and actively used by us, picturing what we give to God.

The temptations in this world are enticing! God has prepared for us all that we need to stand firm. We can have courage in the face of fear. Courage is not the absence of fear; it is taking pro-active action in the face of fear. We want to be a good soldier for Christ.

Let’s take another look at our theme text:

Romans 13:12: (NASB) The night is almost gone, and the day is near. Therefore let us lay aside the deeds of darkness and put on the armor of light.

If we are embroiled in the “deeds of darkness,” our armor of light won’t fit. Satan wants us to think we are battling alone, but we stand shoulder to shoulder with our fellow soldiers.

Ephesians 6:14: (NKJV) Stand therefore, having girded your waist with truth, having put on the breastplate of righteousness… So, whose righteousness are we talking about here?

Romans 3:9-12: (NASB) 9What then? Are we better than they? Not at all; for we have already charged that both Jews and Greeks are all under sin; 10as it is written, There is none righteous, not even one; 11There is none who understands, There is none who seeks for God; 12All have turned aside, together they have become useless; There is none who does good, There is not even one.

The playing field for soldiers is level. No one comes into Christ in a favored state because of their personal “high standing” before God. All are sinners and as such are all worthy of death. We are all broken, battered and bruised but can come together and be armed with the righteousness of Jesus to stand strong.

1 John 2:1-3: (NASB) 1My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. And if anyone sins, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; 2and He Himself is the propitiation for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world. 3By this we know that we have come to know Him, if we keep His commandments.

The righteousness of Jesus protects our vital organs.

Roman Legionary’s clothing (breastplate), Phalera Filmworks - A Legionary soldier was of course well armed, but his body is also very well protected by a helmet, armor (breastplate), and a shield. His body armor is made of iron plates riveted to heavy leather straps on the inside of a harness so they won’t break easily during a fight. When the armor is assembled, he can put it on like a jacket…The breastplate weighs almost 10 kilos (about 22 pounds), but because the different parts move along with the body movement and the weight is spread evenly over the upper body, he can wear it in relative comfort all day long.

Observations about the breastplate:

- This breastplate of righteousness is in fact the righteousness and justification of Jesus.
- It is a weapon of defense, as the Ransom satisfies the just requirements of God and saves us from death.
- For it to protect all of our vital organs it must be attached to us – it must move as we move.
- This breastplate is held in place by the girdle of the truth of God’s plan, for God’s plan is centered on the price that Jesus paid. Wearing this righteousness warrants choices that lead to a dramatic change in our behavior:

2 Corinthians 6:14-18: (NASB) 14Do not be bound together with unbelievers; for what partnership have righteousness and lawlessness, or what fellowship has light with darkness? 15Or what harmony has Christ with Belial, or what has a believer in common with an unbeliever? 16Or what agreement has the temple of God with idols? For we are the temple of the living God; just as God said, I will dwell in them and walk among them; And I will be their God, and they shall be My people. 17Therefore, come out from their midst and be separate, says the Lord. And do not touch what is unclean; And I will welcome you. 18And I will be a father to you, And you shall be sons and daughters to Me, Says the Lord Almighty.

Being a soldier of Christ is a different life – from the inside out. What kind of footwear do we have?

Ephesians 6:15: (NKJV) and having shod your feet with the preparation of the gospel of peace; This seems like an odd statement – your feet wear the “preparation” of the Gospel of peace? Why not wear the Gospel of peace itself?

Roman Legionary’s clothing (sandals), Phalera Filmworks - His military sandals have been cut from a single piece of leather. The thick sole has hobnails. This prevents the sandals from wearing down, and it gives him a firm grip on the slippery soil.

You can buy nearly anything on the internet these days! One website even sells new “Roman Legion sandals” (for $65!) including the hobnails that keep the sole from wearing out too quickly!

First, God is a God of peace:

Romans 16:20: (NASB) The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus be with you.

We can’t win over Satan, but we can fight and in turn God will crush Satan. We win the battle over ourselves by our self-denial and our Christ-likeness. Second, the “good news” of the Gospel confirms that peace and salvation are derived from the plan of the God of peace:

Isaiah 52:7: How beautiful upon the mountains are the feet of him that bringeth good tidings, that publisheth peace; that bringeth good tidings of good that publisheth salvation; that saith unto Zion, Thy God reigneth!

Feet imply you are carrying something, like a delivery person. We carry with us and spread the Gospel of peace. We literally carry that Gospel wherever we go, the “good news.”

Third, the “good news” confirms the pathway to peace and salvation:

2 Corinthians 5:18-20: (NASB) 18Now all these things are from God, who reconciled us to Himself through Christ and gave us the ministry of reconciliation, 19namely, that God was in Christ reconciling the world to Himself, not counting their trespasses against them, and He has committed to us the word of reconciliation. 20Therefore, we are ambassadors for Christ, as though God were making an appeal through us; we beg you on behalf of Christ, be reconciled to God.

Once we, as true Christians, are reconciled to God through Christ, we become ambassadors. Ambassadors live in a foreign country but represent the government of the country from which you came. As an ambassador for Christ, we are coming from the kingdom of God, essentially. We represent that government and carry it to others. There is a pathway to salvation and our responsibility is to show that pathway.

Fourth, to know all of this as a soldier of Christ is to be responsible for it – to be prepared to present it:

1 Peter 3:14-15: (NKJV) 14But even if you should suffer for righteousness sake, you are blessed. And do not be afraid of their threats, nor be troubled. 15But sanctify the Lord God in your hearts, and always be ready to give a defense to everyone who asks you a reason for the hope that is in you, with meekness and fear;

Do you know the truth of God or do you take someone else’s word for it? The idea is to be prepared! We need to know why we believe what we believe. The faith in the Scriptures is not blind.

It is informed, it is intelligent, it has integrity, and it has something concrete to offer! The preparation of the Gospel of peace that we wear on our feet means we are prepared to carry it to our destination.

Fifth, wherever your steps take you, you spread the Gospel.

Romans 10:14-15: (NRSV) 14But how are they to call on one in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in one of whom they have never heard? And how are they to hear without someone to proclaim him? 15And how are they to proclaim him unless they are sent? As it is written, How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news!

We should have such a powerful influence on those around us that people see our kindness, generosity, integrity, and more. These sandals are tied to our feet. They can’t just be kicked off. This is a powerful part of the armor because it carries us to deliver the message of the Gospel in any way possible. Most often it isn’t our words, but it is instead our actions and how we live. So, the message here is simple: Wherever you go, whatever you do, if you are engaged in this battle, one of your responsibilities is to have the “Gospel of Peace” reflected in your every step.

Habakkuk 3:19: The LORD God is my strength, and he will make my feet like hinds’ feet, and he will make me to walk upon mine high places… So, if righteousness is body armor, what protects our brain?

Ephesians 6:17: (NKJV) And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God; (Source: Bible commentator Albert Barnes) The helmet was a cap made of thick leather, or brass, fitted to the head, and was usually crowned with a plume, or crest, as an ornament. Its use was to guard the head from a blow by a sword, or war club, or battle axe.

Obviously, this helmet is there to protect the head, the mind, the attitude, the control center for the entire soldier. How fitting that this protection is made of salvation, for we must have an intellectual acceptance and understanding of the ransom of Jesus on our behalf.

With this understanding in place, we are able to truly focus on the battle at hand.

Isaiah 1:17-18: (NKJV) 17Learn to do good; Seek justice, rebuke the oppressor; Defend the fatherless, plead for the widow. 18Come now, and let us reason together, says the Lord, Though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow; though they are red like crimson, they shall be as wool.

LEARN – SEEK – REBUKE – DEFEND – PLEAD – these have to be protected by salvation. We could easily be taken off course by Satan. Even though we are sinful, we are considered clean in the sight of God because of salvation from the righteousness of Jesus. Our head must be protected by that salvation. This salvation through Jesus should be a primary focus of what we look for in life:

Hebrews 12:2-3: (NASB) 2fixing our eyes on Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God. This salvation through Jesus should be a primary focus of what we meditate on in life: 3For consider him who has endured such hostility by sinners against Himself, so that you will not grow weary and lose heart.

We should be inspired to get up and keep fighting! We should approach the battle with gratitude and thanksgiving that the armor is even available. As long as we do our part, we are invincible until our work is done! Do we see that all of the armor is built around Jesus?

This salvation through Jesus must become part of us:

2 Timothy 2:14-16: (NASB) 14Remind them of these things, and solemnly charge them in the presence of God not to wrangle about words, which is useless and leads to the ruin of the hearers. 15Be diligent to present yourself approved to God as a workman who does not need to be ashamed, accurately handling the word of truth. 16But avoid worldly and empty chatter, for it will lead to further ungodliness, Avoid worldly and empty chatter - the helmet is to focus us clearly on the object at hand.

The pieces of armor are all strapped on and become a part of us. We need to move forward with all the armor on or we are in danger.

So, what does this armor do?

Sandals - bring our feet to a thoughtful delivering of the Gospel. We have to know what we are talking about and be willing to carry it with us.

Breastplate – the righteousness of Jesus that is attached to us, protecting our vital organs. Remember it is put on like a jacket and it protects us with the righteousness of Jesus and not our own.

Belt – the truth that binds all of our protection to us and that holds the sword of the Spirit “at the ready.”

Helmet – The salvation that protects our thoughts, and therefore our deeds, as we go into battle.

Shield – the large external protection of faith that can protect our entire being when necessary. When standing shoulder-to-shoulder with other soldiers, we can create a wall of faith to push back evil.

Sword – God’s own power and influence placed by our side and in our hand to battle an enemy we could never defeat on our own. It is an offensive weapon that is the word of God. We have the responsibility to make sure we strike well and clean. We apply the Spirit of God to the word of God so that it is used appropriately.

The Whole Armor of God: “Don’t leave home without it!”

Got armor?

Mark 4:3: (NASB) Listen to this! ## Episode 708 — Have YOU Ever Been a Prodigal Son?
Published: 2012-05-06
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/parables/708-have-you-ever-been-a-prodigal-son/

Luke 15:11: (NASB) And he said, A man had two sons.

The parable of the Prodigal Son is probably one of the best known of Jesus’ teachings. It touches the heart because of its very practical and dramatic lessons of humility and forgiveness in action. As we look into the story we want to look inward as well. Are we, or have we ever been, prodigal sons? If so, have we come all the way back? And what about the other part of the story – the part we almost never talk about..? Stay with us as we journey through some life changing events!

It’s all about Jesus telling a story... but to whom?

Luke 15:1-3: (NASB) 1Now all the tax collectors and the sinners were coming near him to listen to him. 2Both the Pharisees and the scribes began to grumble, saying, This man receives sinners and eats with them. 3So he told them this parable, saying...

Tax collectors/publicans: The publicans were Jews who had become somewhat estranged from their laws and to the patriotic sentiments of the nation, and who accepted service under the Romans as tax-gatherers. and sinners: The sinners were the more or less immoral, who made no professions of keeping the Mosaic Law, observances of the more sacred rites and ceremonies, holy days, etc. They were Jews by birth but not by practice.

Pharisees and scribes: The scribes and the Pharisees held themselves aloof from the common people—the scribes, because the masses were illiterate; and the Pharisees, under the claim that the people were sinners, cut off from relationship to God. They were the upper level in the religious caste system of the day.

This audience would have been very much at odds with itself, because the listeners were contradictory. The disciples likely were there as well. All of the listening groups would identify with a different part of the story. The story would need to draw in the self-proclaimed leaders quickly, as they would lose interest most easily, while capturing the imaginations of the rest. Jesus was a master at doing this.

Intro, Prodigal Son, Jesus of Nazareth (1977 movie)

Luke 15:11-13: (NASB) 11And he said, A man had two sons. 12The younger of them said to his father, Father, give me the share of the estate that falls to me. So he divided his wealth between them. 13And not many days later, the younger son gathered everything together and went on a journey into a distant country, and there he squandered his estate with loose living. Immediately there is drama and Jesus uses this story to teach the audience about themselves.

The younger son basically collects, leaves and squanders. Sounds like the pursuit of instant gratification! Sound familiar?

Robert “the man," Who needs God, manyviews.org - Robert craved the kind of power and influence held by the mob bosses he idolized.

- "I loved getting hooked up with this wise guy's son and then we started with our own crew. We started taking numbers and things of that nature. That was the step that I took to get considered as an associate into the Gambino crime family." - Soon, Robert gained respect inside New York's criminal underworld. - "I was known as the up and coming star and they would take me and parade me around like that. I truly came to believe that I was a legend in my own mind."

Romans 13:13-14: (NASB) 13Let us behave properly as in the day, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual promiscuity and sensuality, not in strife and jealousy. 14But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh in regard to its lusts.

Famine, Jesus of Nazareth (1977 movie)

Luke 15:14-16: (NASB) 14Now when he had spent everything, a severe famine occurred in that country, and he began to be impoverished. 15So he went and hired himself out to one of the citizens of that country, and he sent him into his fields to feed swine. 16And he would have gladly filled his stomach with the pods that the swine were eating, and no one was giving anything to him.

The son has lost everything and is now feeding swine. For a Jew, this would have been a real disgrace.

Robert the Crackhead, manyviews.org - "And I got attracted to that and thought that was the next level up. But I got caught up with the coke itself and I would do more than I sold and eventually I would owe them money and I started running out of resources of people giving me coke because I owed everybody money. That's when crack started being big, and it was cheaper." - Crack consumed him. It cost him his reputation and everything Robert had worked for. - "I started realizing this was like the point of hopelessness. Okay, I'm Robert the Crackhead and I will die Robert the Crackhead."

Who were the two sons? All of the nation of Israel were God’s children:

Amos 3:1-2: (NRSV) 1Hear this word that the LORD has spoken against you, O people of Israel, against the whole family that I brought up out of the land of Egypt: 2You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.

The Characters

Who did they represent?

Observation

The Lessons for Us Older son, more privileged and stable The self- proclaimed "elite" of Israel The Pharisees and scribes must have liked this story so far – they would have seen themselves as the faithful son, favored and home while the rebellious son was now poor, miserable and alone.

A sure sign of a prideful heart is finding satisfaction in another’s misfortune.

Younger son, less favored and more rebellious The "sinners" of Israel Sometimes we have great blessings and opportunities that we do not even recognize, much less appreciate. This can often happen when we are given these blessings at an early age, or when we are born into them. "Thank before you think." Assume gratitude and then think through what you will do. Appreciate first and then move forward with other parts of your life. It will focus us on what is most important.

The Father God The father in his wisdom sees the thankless rebellion in his younger son's heart and knows that his stubbornness must give birth to its own actions which in turn will provide the opportunity for learning humility.

This son, having truly found himself, goes home.

His father in his wisdom had let this son go and now in his wisdom is and has been looking for this son’s return. The Lessons for Us

Younger son's resolution

This younger son finally realizes reality. He resolves to go back to his Father. "I will get up and go" – the word for “get up” is often used relating to “rising up,” as in resurrection. This son rehearses his repentance speech: he has sinned against heaven, he has lived a life entirely out of harmony with God, and therefore he has sinned before his father who was a righteous man. His judgment upon himself is to be stripped of his son-ship and to become as a “hired hand.” The severity of this self-judgment shows the sincerity of his repentance.

The truest values in life can only be realized when we have been humbled to such a point that our eye for life is no longer seeking external events full of thrill and excitement, but has been brought to a new level of vision, a level of clear sight, a level of insight. It is at this point that we can once again go home. "Make me as a hired hand" shows complete attitude overhaul. He started the story with an authoritative demand to “give me” and returns with a humble plea for his father’s authority to reinstate him in a vastly reduced position.

A bit on the celebratory elements that the father used to welcome his son back: (Source: Wycliffe Commentary) The fatted calf. One animal was usually held in readiness for a special occasion, that honored guests might be served quickly. Be merry (celebrate) has the connotation of a party. Music and dancing were probably supplied by hired entertainers. The return of the younger son was cause for a major celebration.

(Source: Dr. Robert Anthony) It helps to realize that an airplane spends 90% of its time in error. We need to take a look at that. If you could see that you could get an airplane from New York to London, even while having been in error ninety percent of the time, maybe you could be less critical of yourself... A sailboat cannot get from where it is to where it wants to be by traveling in a straight line. It has to zigzag. So in terms of true course, it’s always in error. What is important about an airplane or a sailboat is that the errors cancel out.

Similarly, God’s plan accounts for the errors of sin and will in fact guide humanity towards its ultimate destination!

So, what IS the ultimate destination for the sin weary world of humankind? So, what do we know about God and his permitting tragedy upon the earth?

- It is only temporary!
- It has a purpose – to display the sorrow and hopelessness of sin and death. It displays what happens when God is not in the picture.
- It reveals the folly of life under the rule of Satan. God knew it would serve an ultimate, eternal purpose.
- It leads to the end of this order of things (governments, false religions, false Christian beliefs, etc.).
- It opens the door to the new order. So, from trouble comes purity:

Zephaniah 3:8-9: (NRSV) 8Therefore wait for me, says the LORD, for the day when I arise as a witness. For my decision is to gather nations, to assemble kingdoms, to pour out upon them my indignation, all the heat of my anger; for in the fire of my passion all the earth shall be consumed. 9At that time I will change the speech of the peoples to a pure speech, that all of them may call on the name of the LORD and serve him with one accord.

Satan's evil order will end.

From trouble comes peace on earth:

Isaiah 11:5-9: (NASB) 7Also the cow and the bear will graze, their young will lie down together, and the lion will eat straw like the ox. 8The nursing child will play by the hole of the cobra, and the weaned child will put his hand on the viper’s den. 9They will not hurt or destroy in all My holy mountain, for the earth will be full of the knowledge of the LORD as the waters cover the sea.

This text speaks of Jesus and his kingdom. Prophecy says the future will be completely different from the present. It will be the world God intended it to be. There will be peace on the earth. If God promises it, it will come true.

From trouble comes unity:

Zechariah 8:20-23: (KJV) 20Thus saith the LORD of hosts; It shall yet come to pass, that there shall come people, and the inhabitants of many cities: 21And the inhabitants of one city shall go to another, saying, Let us go speedily to pray before the LORD, and to seek the LORD of hosts: I will go also. 22Yea, many people and strong nations shall come to seek the LORD of hosts in Jerusalem, and to pray before the LORD. 23Thus saith the LORD of hosts; In those days it shall come to pass, that ten men shall take hold out of all languages of the nations, even shall take hold of the skirt of him that is a Jew, saying, We will go with you: for we have heard that God is with you.

All the nations together will join together in praying before the Lord. Notice the Jewish people are an important part in the unfolding of God's plan. Jerusalem is the holy city and God will fight for the Jews.

Acts 3:19-21: 19...when the times of refreshing shall come from the presence of the Lord: 20And he shall send Jesus Christ, which before was preached unto you: 21Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things, which God hath spoken by the mouth of all his holy prophets since the world began.

Revelation 21:3-4: (KJV) 3And I heard a great voice out of heaven saying, Behold, the tabernacle of God is with men, (not just Christians, not just Jews) and he will dwell with them, and they shall be his people, and God himself shall be with them, and be their God. 4And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.

The "former things" have passed away - sin, dying, injustice, evil. This gives us great hope.

Romans 5:18-19: (NRSV) 18Therefore just as one man's trespass led to condemnation for all, so one man's act of righteousness leads to justification and life for all. 19For just as by the one man's disobedience the many were made sinners, so by the one man's obedience the many will be made righteous.

## Episode 1341 — What Did Jesus Mean When He Talked About Hellfire? (Hellfire Series Part I)
Published: 2024-07-08
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1341-gehenna/

What Did Jesus Mean When He Talked About Hellfire? (Hellfire Series Part I)

Mark 9:47–48: If your eye causes you to stumble, throw it out; it is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye, than, having two eyes, to be cast into hell, 48 where THEIR WORM DOES NOT DIE, AND THE FIRE IS NOT QUENCHED.

To the critical observer, modern Christianity is confusing, as we have countless denominations and their countless ways of interpreting Scripture. These widely varied interpretations give birth to widely varied traditions that support those interpretations. As a major subset of this, we have wide discrepancies regarding the destiny of unbelievers. Several times, Jesus plainly taught about the consequences of hell. The enormous question that needs answering is, did he teach that hell was a place of agonizing and eternal torture from which there is no escape, or were his several references to hell pointing to a very different meaning? Today’s focus will be on the primary New Testament word Jesus used to describe hell. If we understand the word and its context, we will understand Jesus’ meaning. What is our position on hell as a place of eternal, conscious torment? Our position is that hell is NOT a place of eternal torment. This is NOT scriptural. It is NOT what Jesus taught. He was talking about something entirely different. Why do we say that when over a thousand years of tradition―and superstition―say otherwise?

This is why this is such an important topic. Scriptures from both Old and New Testaments are in profound harmony and provide clarity when we put them together. Let’s begin by quoting three different plain statements of Jesus that are representative of his teachings about hell.

He spoke these words to his followers:

Mark 9:43,47–48: 43 If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off; it is better for you to enter life crippled, than, having your two hands, to go into hell <1067>, into the unquenchable <762> fire. 47 If your eye causes you to stumble, throw it out; it is better for you to enter the kingdom of God with one eye, than, having two eyes, to be cast into hell <1067>, 48 where THEIR WORM DOES NOT DIE, AND THE FIRE IS NOT QUENCHED <4570>.

Unquenchable: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #762 asbestos; a derivative of #4570; not extinguished—not to be quenched He spoke these words to the scribes and Pharisees:

Matthew 23:29,32-33: 29 Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! For you build the tombs of the prophets and adorn the monuments of the righteous, 32 Fill up, then, the measure of the guilt of your fathers. 33 You serpents, you brood of vipers, how will you escape the sentence of hell <1067>?

This sounds pretty ominous!

Again, he spoke to his followers:

Matthew 10:28 (KJV): And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy <622> (to destroy fully) both soul and body in hell <1067>.

We see the word hell again and again in these three scripture references. There are a few others, but these are representative of the rest.

In the scriptures we have quoted, Jesus used the Greek word Gehenna. This word refers to an actual location—the Valley of the Son of Hinnom.

Hell: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1067: geenna; valley of (the son of) Hinnom; ge-henna (or Ge-Hinnom), a valley of Jerusalem Gehenna is the Valley of Hinnom. What happened there? (Source: Nelson's Illustrated Bible Dictionary) In the time of Jesus the Valley of Hinnom was used as the garbage dump of Jerusalem. Into it were thrown all the filth and garbage of the city, including the dead bodies of animals and executed criminals. To consume all this, fires burned constantly. Maggots worked in the filth. When the wind blew from that direction over the city, its awfulness was quite evident. (Source: Albert Barnes’ Notes on the Whole Bible) The Jew's extreme loathsomeness of the place, the filth and putrefaction, the corruption of the atmosphere, and the lurid fires blazing by day and night, made it one of the most appalling symbols with which a Jew was acquainted.

This is the traditional explanation. This is being questioned among scholars because archeologists haven’t actually found evidence of this garbage dump, and it’s not mentioned in early literary writings―at least those that have survived. But let’s assume for a moment Jesus was alluding to this.

Is Jesus saying if you speak slanderously of your brother, or if you lust in your heart or act hypocritically or sinfully, your penalty is to be burned up at the local dump? Was there something about this particular valley—the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (which incidentally was on earth, not inside the earth) that made it worthy to be a specific example used by Jesus over and over again? This particular valley was well-known by the Jewish people for very specific and traumatic reasons:

Jeremiah 19:2–6 (KJV): 2 And go forth unto the valley of the son of Hinnom, which is by the entry of the east gate, and proclaim there the words that I shall tell thee, 3 And say, Hear ye the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah, and inhabitants of Jerusalem; thus saith the LORD of hosts, the God of Israel; behold, I will bring evil upon this place, the which whosoever heareth, his ears shall tingle.

God proclaims through the prophet Jeremiah that He will bring evil upon this place and whoever hears this will have ringing in their ears—it will be something very dramatic! 4 Because they have forsaken me, and have estranged this place, and have burned incense in it unto other gods, whom neither they nor their fathers have known, nor the kings of Judah, and have filled this place with the blood of innocents; It was a place of serious, overt idolatry. This is the first proclamation of condemnation to this piece of land. Israel had used it as a centerpiece for idolatry, breaking the fundamental truth of the First Commandment God had taught them, You shall have no other gods before Me (Exodus 20:3). 5 they have built also the high places of Baal, to burn their sons with fire for burnt offerings unto Baal, which I commanded not, nor spake it, neither came it into my mind: They sacrificed their children by burning them alive to the pagan god, Baal, in this idolatrous practice.

God’s response is, This is what happens with My chosen people?!? You do this awful thing? This never even came into My mind! This is so far off from anything resembling godliness and righteousness! God could not even imagine this evil they were practicing. 6 Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the LORD, that this place shall no more be called Tophet, nor the valley of the son of Hinnom, but the valley of slaughter. In Jewish history, this valley was first named the valley of the son of Hinnom after its owners in the times of Joshua. It became known as Tophet because of the child sacrifices that occurred there. Scholars aren’t sure of the origin of this word. It could be Aramaic (taphya) meaning “hearth” or “fire-place,” and the Old Testament links it several times to a place of ritual fire or burning. Some older Bible commentaries suggest it comes from a

Hebrew word toph meaning “drum,” referencing the beating of drums to block out the cries of the babies.

Verse 6 says now it would be called the Valley of Slaughter. God is repeating Jeremiah 7:31-32—because of the idolatry of Judah and this horrific practice of human sacrifice, they would be overrun by their enemies and their dead corpses would be eaten by animals instead of buried. This would have been extremely shameful for the Hebrews. All of this history is wrapped up in this Valley of Hinnom, or Gehenna. This is the place Jesus is speaking of, and there is nothing good about these descriptions.

Jeremiah 19:7 (KJV): And I will make void the counsel of Judah and Jerusalem in this place; and I will cause them to fall by the sword before their enemies, and by the hands of them that seek their lives: and their carcasses will I give to be meat for the fowls of the heaven, and for the beasts of the earth.

This is why the name was changed to the Valley of Slaughter.

Is this showing eternal destruction or eternal conscious pain?

When Jesus uses the word Gehenna, many Christians interpret it as meaning eternal conscious pain. But when we look at the Old Testament scriptures that give the history of why this valley became such a heinous symbol before God, we don’t see that. Rather, we see a symbol of eternal destruction. Verse 7 says their carcasses will I give to be meat for the fowls of the heaven. There is no torture or consciousness here—they are dead bodies left for the carrion birds and beasts of the earth.

The New Testament Gehenna encompassed all that we have just discussed. It first became a place of heinous idolatry and then a place of death, defeat and dishonor. God proclaimed Gehenna to be a place of FINAL and COMPLETE DESTRUCTION!

To sum up, Jesus used the Greek word, Gehenna, translated into English as hell. His listeners would have been familiar with this infamous location of death and destruction and would have understood what he meant.

This phrase was used very specifically in several Old Testament scriptures. Its meaning was focused on a fire that would burn until its work was unequivocally completed. The fire burns until there is nothing left to burn—it runs out of fuel.

We have two examples: Idumaeans were descendants of Jacob’s brother Esau, known as the Edomites. Idumaea is a Greek name for Edom. Herod the Great, who tried to kill the infant Jesus, was an Idumaean.

The desolation of the city of Idumaea:

Isaiah 34:8–10: 8 For the LORD has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense for the cause of Zion. 9 Its streams will be turned into pitch (tar, asphalt), and its loose earth into brimstone (sulfur), and its land will become burning pitch.

Fire destroys what it consumes. Brimstone intensifies the

destructive aspect when added to fire, as sulfur fumes are toxic and deadly. Fire and brimstone together symbolically emphasize the severity of the destruction. 10 It will not be quenched (extinguished) night or day; its smoke will go up forever. From generation to generation it will be desolate; none will pass through it forever and ever. This burning will never be quenched, never be extinguished.

This text has both literal and prophetic fulfillments. There was a literal battle in ancient times, AND it is part of the future day of vengeance prophecies. This phrase, the Lord has a day of vengeance, a year of recompense has a double fulfillment―the first taking place at the time of the prophecy and the second sometime in the future.

We know the day of vengeance in the time of the end is a day of great destruction of the systems here on earth. This description fits well with the unquenchable fire representing the full and complete judgment of sin. The people were sinful and were annihilated. When fire and brimstone (or sulfur) are brought together, nothing lives. Everything dies.

We know for sure it’s NOT from present-day archeological digs of where the Idumaeans lived, so it is NOT burning today. If it’s not still burning, why does the scripture say it will burn forever? How was the word meant to be used?

Unquenchable meant the fire would burn―unable to be put out or quenched―until its work was done.

Today we might say, I have an unquenchable thirst to describe when we are really thirsty. Does it go on and on forever? No, just until we drink something and are satisfied.

Another modern day example, “She has an unquenchable desire for knowledge,” meaning she wants to learn more and more.

Jesus used Old Testament examples to create New Testament teachings. This is a powerful thought to keep in mind. Often when Old Testament words are brought forth into the New Testament their meaning doesn’t change, even if the lesson expands. These prophecies show devastating destruction but no eternal torment.

The overthrow of the Jews and the laying waste of Judea by Nebuchadnezzar and the Chaldeans:

Ezekiel 20:47–48: 47 and say to the forest of the Negev, Hear the word of the LORD: thus says the Lord GOD, Behold, I am about to kindle a fire in you, and it will consume every green tree in you, as well as every dry tree; the blazing flame will not be quenched <3518> and the whole surface from south to north will be burned by it. 48 All flesh will see that I, the LORD, have kindled it; it shall not be quenched <3518>.

Quenched: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3518 kāḇâ; to expire or (causatively) to extinguish (fire, light, anger):—go (put) out, quench

Let’s paraphrase the scripture: I will say to the forest, “This is what is going to happen. There will be a fire that will consume every green tree as well as every dry tree.” It is unquenchable, because nobody can stop it by putting it out.

When a wildfire can’t be put out, everything gets destroyed. The fire only goes out when there is nothing left to consume. The fuel is gone. So, no, the blazing flame of Ezekiel 20:47 is not still burning today. Why? Because the unquenchable fire did exactly what it was there for.

These Old Testament examples help us understand the language Jesus uses in the New Testament.

Isaiah 1:31, Jeremiah 4:4 and Amos 5:6 also promise “unquenchable” fires that have long ago burned out.

When we say somebody has unquenchable thirst, it indicates a condition exists until it is brought under control. With forest fires, the forest burns until the fuel is gone and there is nothing left to burn. It is done. This is what these scriptures are telling us. There are definitely Old Testament references to God’s wrath in conjunction with fire, brimstone and worms, but nothing is said or hinted at about eternal conscious torture as a punishment for not believing in Jesus as our ransom sacrifice now in this lifetime. Millions of people were born before Jesus came to earth. There is nothing in the Bible that says God will torture them eternally for being born too early.

We have to put the concept of eternal flames into the context of Scripture as a whole. The Old and New Testaments are both parts of the whole; they must be interpreted together. Jesus and the apostles frequently quoted the Old Testament, referring to established scriptural ideas.

John the Baptist spoke of Jesus and used this same symbolic Old Testament language. In the previous verse (Matthew 3:11), John just said someone (Jesus) is coming after him who is so much mightier than John that John isn’t even fit to remove his sandals. Jesus would baptize with the holy spirit and ﬁre―two diﬀerent things. “Baptism of fire” means judgment and trouble.

Matthew 3:12: His winnowing fork is in his hand, and he will thoroughly clear his threshing floor; and he will gather his wheat into the barn, but he will burn up the chaff with unquenchable <762> fire.

John is talking about what was going to happen to the nation of Israel. He is there to pave the way for Jesus, talking about the many who would reject Jesus. As a consequence, Israel would be destroyed as a nation.

Is the fire of Israel’s destruction as a nation still burning today? No. John was talking in symbolic language of the nation of Israel. There were a few individual Jews drawn to Jesus who became “wheat” and part of his true church, the body of Christ that will bless all of mankind. But the nation itself ended up being “chaff,” and therefore was destroyed. It is not still burning today. Israel rejected Jesus and was literally destroyed as a nation in 70AD. There was no nation of Israel after that time. This destruction was complete. The “fire” went out because there was nothing left to burn until the time when God called the “dry bones” of Israel to life! Ezekiel 37 gives us the picture of a valley of dry bones. Nothing in that valley was alive. Yet, God would call these dry bones back to life. It was a picture of Israel as the re-establishment of Israel as a nation. They were destroyed as chaff but God brought them back to life. This prophecy was fulfilled when Israel again became a nation in 1948.

The prophecy of the destruction and rebirth of Israel as a nation gives us a beautiful picture of how unquenchable is used in the Bible. Out of death, God made life for this nation.

Let’s go back to Jesus’ own words regarding “unquenchable” related to the language of the day:

Mark 9:43: If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off; it is better for you to enter life crippled, than, having your two hands, to go into hell <1067> (Gehenna), into the unquenchable <762> fire,

We showed how unquenchable fire represents complete destruction. Total destruction is the biblical end for the incorrigible—the absolutely sinful. Both Old and New Testaments attest to this. Had it not been for Jesus, the Old Testament destruction of any people or nation would have been a permanent result. The point?

When Jesus came, he paid the price to ransom every human being so they have the opportunity to come back to life and back to God. When Jesus talks about his followers who sin, he warns it is better for them to stop whatever they are doing even if it hurts (If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off—symbolically cutting ourselves off from whatever stumbles us), so they do not end up in a very untenable, disloyal and ungodly circumstance that will make them subject to that destructive fire.

Unquenchable means until its work was done―until it runs out of fuel. Jesus didn’t change the meaning of this word.

Jesus referred to Gehenna, historically a place of death and destruction.

Are there really magic worms that live forever?

Jesus talks about two things here—unusual worms and determined fire:

Mark 9:48: where THEIR WORM DOES NOT DIE, AND THE FIRE IS NOT QUENCHED.

A fire that is not quenched means no one puts it out; it eventually burns out when it runs out of fuel. We see a connection in the meaning to the worms that don’t die since the two phrases are connected in this scripture.

Jesus quoted from:

Isaiah 66:23–24: 23 And it shall be from new moon to new moon and from sabbath to sabbath, all mankind will come to bow down before Me, says the LORD (obviously a prophecy of a future time―mankind has never all bowed down). 24 Then they will go forth and look (meaning “to see,” literally or figuratively) on the corpses of the men who have transgressed against Me. For their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched; and they will be an abhorrence to all mankind.

Corpses are dead. This Hebrew word means a carcass, or when used figuratively, it means an idolatrous image. Even if someone were to take this literally, the prophecy does NOT include torture.

Then they will go forth and look—when we “see” something in our mind, it means we understand it. The image of worms that don’t die and a fire that is not quenched is the recollection of what sin produces. The awful memory of the effects of evil will inspire people to maintain a heart condition of loyalty and honor to God in the kingdom. They will remember the pain of death and destruction.

Adam’s sin condemned himself and all mankind to death—dying thou shalt die. Had it not been for Jesus’ sacrifice, the human race would have remained in the grave permanently. In God’s future kingdom, all mankind will bow down before God, never forgetting the destructiveness of sin. This is a sad and age-lasting reminder of the destruction of those who ultimately stood against God.

The New Testament follows the Old Testament in teaching about complete destruction. Let’s look at some examples from Jesus, the Apostle Peter and the Apostle Paul. The following texts introduce different Greek words translated as destruction. Jesus’ words:

Matthew 10:28 (KJV): And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy <622> both soul and body in hell <1067>.

Destroy: Thayer’s Greek Lexicon #622 apollumi; to destroy fully (reflexively, to perish, or lose), literally or figuratively

Jesus is speaking about utter destruction after he ransomed us, referring to what Revelation labels as the second death (Revelation 20:14), not torture.

In Matthew 10:28, Jesus is talking to his followers, telling them that once they are justified and receive the holy spirit (God’s power and influence), they will follow in his footsteps. But if they were to turn their backs on him and deny him, they will be destroyed in second death. Not tortured, tormented or teased. Utterly destroyed. That is what the Valley of Hinnom was all about!

Acts 3:23 (KJV): And it shall come to pass, that every soul, which will not hear that prophet, shall be destroyed <1842> from among the people.

Destroyed: Thayer’s Greek Lexicon #1842: exolothreuo; to extirpate Thayer’s Greek-English Lexicon: 1a: to destroy completely: wipe out 1b: to pull up by the root 2: to cut out by surgery

Jesus’ words again:

Matthew 7:13 (KJV): Enter ye in at the strait gate: for wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction <#684>, and many there be which go in thereat: Destruction: Thayer’s Greek Lexicon #684 apoleia; ruin or loss (physical, spiritual or eternal)

Philippians 3:19 (KJV): Whose end is destruction <684>, whose God is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame…

The Scriptures from beginning to end have this theme of destruction, not torment, as verified by Jesus and his apostles.

Let’s sum all of this up with another prophecy:

Zephaniah 3:8–9: 8 Therefore wait for Me, declares the LORD, For the day when I rise up as a witness. Indeed, My decision is to gather nations, to assemble kingdoms, to pour out on them My indignation, all My burning anger; for all the earth will be devoured by the fire of My zeal.

If we didn’t know better, we would use this as proof of eternal torment! However, read on: 9 For then I will give to the peoples purified lips, that all of them may call on the name of the LORD, to serve Him shoulder to shoulder.

Ah—here’s the other function fire serves. It destroys, but it can also purify. Once the dross is burned off, the gold remains. Purified lips aren’t calling on the Lord and serving Him while being eternally tortured.

These scriptures and definitions explain why we say eternal torment is NOT taught in Scripture. Jesus expands the established Old Testament theme and used it to show us the depth of loyalty necessary for God’s people to show to Him.

Jesus taught the gospel based on the foundation of Old Testament teachings, fitting them together in relation to his mission―the call of the true church. His descriptions of utter destruction fit precisely with Jewish history and prophetic writings. God proclaimed the Valley of Hinnom to be known as the Valley of Slaughter and not the Valley of Torment for good reason, as it would depict the ultimate consequence for anyone who defies God to the very end.

It is important to understand that the Old and New Testaments work in perfect harmony with one another. Destruction was taught in the Old Testament, and Jesus taught it in the New Testament. Let us not get stuck in the traditions of men; let us stick with the truth of Scripture.

So, what did Jesus mean when he talked about hellfire?

## Episode 764 — What Does it Mean to be Merciful?
Published: 2013-06-02
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/764-what-does-it-mean-to-be-merciful/

Lamentations 3:22–23: (KJV) 22It is of the LORD’s mercies that we are not consumed, because his compassions fail not. 23They are new every morning: great is thy faithfulness.

Sometimes in the overwhelming flow of life we can forget the simplest things. We get so caught up in a “me first” – and sometimes a “me only” mentality that it never even crosses our minds to stop and consider some of the most basic and healing attributes available to humankind – kindness and mercy. What is mercy? How does it work? If we were to apply mercy on a regular basis, would it change our world and more importantly, could it change the way we see our world?

What is mercy?

Old Testament:

Micah 6:8: (KJV) He hath showed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy <2617>, and to walk humbly with thy God?

Kindness/Mercy: Strongs #2617, goodness, kindness, faithfulness

Hosea 6:6: (NASB) For I delight in loyalty <2617> rather than sacrifice, and in the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.

The word for loyalty here is the same as was previously translated mercy! We will develop this further, but your loyalty to a person can draw you to a point of mercy.

Introduction, Diane Sawyer, ABC News (2008) (Susan Atkins killed for Charles Manson and gave this interview from prison before her death.) - …this was an event so terrifying; it changed America…one of the most infamous murders in the U.S. And now, the young woman involved is asking for freedom after 37 years in prison. Susan Atkins was a member of the Manson family convicted in the 1969 murder of actress Sharon Tate and four others. Now, she has brain cancer and doctors say she has just months to live. She is raising questions about mercy, then and now.

New Testament:

Matthew 5:7: (NRSV) Blessed are the merciful, for they will receive mercy <1653>.

Mercy: Strongs #1653 el-eh-eh’-o; to be compassionate (by word or deed, specially, by divine grace): have compassion (pity on), have (obtain, receive, shew) mercy (on). Another word translated “mercy” in English: Mercy: Strongs #1656 eleov eleos el’-eh-os

1) mercy: kindness or goodwill towards the miserable and the afflicted, joined with a desire to help them 1a) of men towards men: to exercise the virtue of mercy, show one’s self merciful 1b) of God towards men: in general providence; the mercy and clemency of God in providing and offering to men salvation by Christ When there is misery, mercy takes a role to alleviate such misery.

Oftentimes we look at God’s grace as being an overview of all that God does for us, but mercy and grace are actually different. They work together.

Mercy in action:

Matthew 9:9-13: (NASB) 9As Jesus went on from there, he saw a man called Matthew, sitting in the tax collector’s booth; and he said to him, Follow me! And he got up and followed him.10Then it happened that as Jesus was reclining at the table in the house, behold, many tax collectors and sinners came and were dining with Jesus and his disciples. 11When the Pharisees saw this, they said to his disciples, Why is your Teacher eating with the tax collectors and sinners? 12But when Jesus heard this, he said, It is not those who are healthy who need a physician, but those who are sick. 13But go and learn what this means: I desire compassion <1656>, and not sacrifice, (Jesus here quoting Hosea 6:6) for I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners.

What must mercy be based upon?

Point of interest: The vast majority of scriptures that talk about mercy are focused on the mercy of God to man. There are but a few scriptures that talk about human mercy towards each other.

There are several texts that link mercy and justice together for us:

Micah 6:8: (KJV) He hath showed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?

Hosea 12:5-6: (NASB) 5Even the LORD, the God of hosts, the LORD is His name. 6Therefore, return to your God, observe kindness and justice, and wait for your God continually.

Mercy in action:

Matthew 20:29-34: (NASB) 29As they were leaving Jericho, a large crowd followed him. 30And two blind men sitting by the road, hearing that Jesus was passing by, cried out, Lord, have mercy on us, Son of David! 31The crowd sternly told them to be quiet, but they cried out all the more, Lord, Son of David, have mercy on us! 32And Jesus stopped and called them, and said, What do you want me to do for you? 33They said to him, Lord, we want our eyes to be opened. 34Moved with compassion, Jesus touched their eyes; and immediately they regained their sight and followed him.

Mercy changes others’ circumstances when it was not required to be rendered, so it is an important action we can and should take.

But how was that healing based in justice?

Isaiah 61:1: (NASB) The Spirit of the Lord GOD is upon me, because the LORD has anointed me to bring good news to the afflicted; He has sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to captives and freedom to prisoners; Jesus quoted this verse in the Temple and confirmed that it was about him.

Jesus fulfilled the just plan of God by coming to show this would be a permanent change in the future. Jesus was moved with compassion. He felt for them and changed their circumstances by giving of himself.

How does God’s mercy express itself?

Psalms 36:5-12: (NASB) 5Your lovingkindness (mercy), O LORD, extends to the heavens, your faithfulness reaches to the skies. 6Your righteousness is like the mountains of God; Your judgments are like a great deep. O LORD, You preserve man and beast. 7How precious is Your lovingkindness (mercy), O God! And the children of men take refuge in the shadow of Your wings. 8They drink their fill of the abundance of Your house; And You give them to drink of the river of Your delights. 9For with You is the fountain of life; In Your light we see light. 10O continue Your lovingkindness (mercy) to those who know You, and Your righteousness to the upright in heart. 11Let not the foot of pride come upon me, and let not the hand of the wicked drive me away.

God’s mercy surrounds the earth, protects the feeble and is reachable as long as we do not allow our own pride or another’s wickedness to interfere. God’s mercy has different levels of expression. It is fully expressed through the ransom of Jesus, as we will discuss later. For believers and followers of Jesus, God’s mercies are already apparent. For “everybody else,” it is yet to come.

1 Peter 1:3-5: (NASB) 3Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to His great mercy <1656> has caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead, 4to obtain an inheritance which is imperishable and undefiled and will not fade away, reserved in heaven for you, 5who are protected by the power of God through faith for a salvation ready to be revealed in the last time.

God’s mercy is expressed through the death and resurrection of Jesus and that leads to heavenly inheritance! It all comes back to the love of God.

Discipleship in Christ is the precursor of what is to come to everyone else. It is given to the true follower of Christ ahead of time to those. It is given to those who have dedicated themselves to Christ in a time when it is not convenient or easy, and at a time when people laugh at you. But it is such a privilege and an expression of God’s mercy and then grace!

God’s love had to be first, because that is what created a just environment.

Titus 3:4-7: (NRSV) 4But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, 5he saved us, not because of any works of righteousness that we had done, but according to his mercy <1656>, through the water of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit. 6This Spirit he poured out on us richly through Jesus Christ our Savior, 7so that, having been justified by his grace, we might become heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

Hebrews 4:14-16: (NASB) 14Therefore, since we have a great high priest who has passed through the heavens, Jesus the Son of God, let us hold fast our confession. 15For we do not have a high priest who cannot sympathize with our weaknesses, but One who has been tempted in all things as we are, yet without sin. 16Therefore let us draw near with confidence to the throne of grace, so that we may receive mercy (an action) and (then you are able to) find grace to help in time of need.

Yet another connection for mercy – this time it is grace.

What is the difference between mercy and grace?

Both are undeserved, but one is compassion and one is favor.

Mercy in action:

Luke 10:30-37: (NASB) 30Jesus replied and said, A man was going down from Jerusalem to Jericho, and fell among robbers, and they stripped him and beat him, and went away leaving him half dead...33But a Samaritan, who was on a journey, came upon him; and when he saw him, he felt compassion, 34and came to him and bandaged up his wounds, pouring oil and wine on them; and he put him on his own beast, and brought him to an inn and took care of him. 35On the next day he took out two denarii and gave them to the innkeeper and said, Take care of him; and whatever more you spend, when I return I will repay you. 36Which of these three do you think proved to be a neighbor to the man who fell into the robbers’ hands? 37And he said, The one who showed mercy <1656> toward him. How do we express mercy?

In the following teaching, is Jesus telling us to give people what they deserve?

Luke 6:27-36: (NASB) 27But I say to you who hear, love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, 28bless those who curse you, pray for those who mistreat you. 29Whoever hits you on the cheek, offer him the other also; (do not retaliate; remember this does not have to be a physical hit) and whoever takes away your coat, do not withhold your shirt from him either. (give to those who take) 30Give to everyone who asks of you, and whoever takes away what is yours, do not demand it back. (give to those in need) 31Treat others the same way you want them to treat you. (live justly) 32If you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them. 33If you do good to those who do good to you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners do the same. 34If you lend to those from whom you expect to receive, what credit is that to you? Even sinners lend to sinners in order to receive back the same amount. (live a higher standard) 35But love your enemies, and do good, and lend, expecting nothing in return; and your reward will be great, and you will be sons of the Most High; for He Himself is kind to ungrateful and evil men. 36Be merciful, just as your Father is merciful. God’s mercy and grace is a template for us to follow in dealing with others.

Living remorse, Susan Atkins interview with Diane Sawyer, ABC (2002) - (Sawyer) Sharon Tate’s father, Paul, wrote: “31 years ago, I sat in a courtroom with a jury and watched with others and saw a young woman who giggled, sniffled and shouted out insults. While testifying about my daughter’s last breath, she laughed.” What argument can you make to him? - (Atkins) There is none. There is only the continued attempt to apologize to him. Remorse is genuine repentance, turning away from behavior… Here is a great parable regarding kindness and mercy:

Matthew 18:23-33: (NASB) 23For this reason the kingdom of heaven may be compared to a king who wished to settle accounts with his slaves. 24When he had begun to settle them, one who owed him ten thousand talents was brought to him. 25But since he did not have the means to repay, his lord commanded him to be sold, along with his wife and children and all that he had, and repayment to be made. 26So the slave fell to the ground and prostrated himself before him, saying, Have patience with me and I will repay you everything. 27And the lord of that slave felt compassion and released him and forgave him the debt. 28But that slave went out and found one of his fellow slaves who owed him a hundred denarii; and he seized him and began to choke him, saying, Pay back what you owe. 29So his fellow slave fell to the ground and began to plead with him, saying, Have patience with me and I will repay you. 30But he was unwilling and went and threw him in prison until he should pay back what was owed. 31So when his fellow slaves saw what had happened, they were deeply grieved and came and reported to their lord all that had happened. 32Then summoning him, his lord said to him, You wicked slave, I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me. 33Should you not also have had mercy <1653> on your fellow slave, in the same way that I had mercy <1653> on you?’ We can live mercifully by:

- Claiming the mercy of God on our behalf
- Appreciating the mercy of God on our behalf
- Realizing the magnitude of God’s mercy on our behalf related to our small earthly issues
- Extending the mercy of God on our behalf to those over whom we have power Is mercy always appropriate? Everyone lost, Susan Atkins interview with Diane Sawyer, ABC (2002) - I don’t want to live a life with any unforgiveness in it. So many people lost so much. The victims, the families of the victims, the families of the people who were involved, the community at large, the society at large. Everybody lost. We agree that she should not have been paroled. Justice needed to be met. However, we believe God’s mercy worked in her by helping her to transform her life where she was.

A caller suggested: Romans 12:21: Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good.

Israel’s command towards mercy:

Zechariah 7:8-14: (NASB) 8Then the word of the LORD came to Zechariah saying, 9Thus has the LORD of hosts said, Dispense true justice and practice kindness <2617> and compassion each to his brother; 10and do not oppress the widow or the orphan, the stranger or the poor; and do not devise evil in your hearts against one another. 11But they refused to pay attention and turned a stubborn shoulder and stopped their ears from hearing. 12They made their hearts like flint so that they could not hear the law and the words which the LORD of hosts had sent by His Spirit through the former prophets; therefore great wrath came from the LORD of hosts. 13And just as He called and I would not listen, says the LORD of hosts; 14but I scattered them with a storm wind among all the nations whom they have not known. Thus the land is desolated behind them so that no one went back and forth, for they made the pleasant land desolate.

They were told to live by the law but practice mercy. They refused to listen and the consequence was the desolation of the land. God’s mercy was withdrawn because they did not show mercy to others. We really need to be thinking “mercy first” wherever possible.

Romans 9:14-15: (NASB) 14What shall we say then? There is no injustice with God, is there? May it never be! 15For He says to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I have compassion.

God is not compelled to show all mercy in all circumstances, yet here He does show His willingness. Does He have mercy on all of His creation? Yes, because His plan, set up before the foundation of the earth, shows the sacrifice for sin even before the sin happened. That ransom satisfied justice, allowing mercy to eventually flourish.

For right now during the unfolding of His plan, God can pick and choose where His mercy applies and where it does not apply. Is that unjust? No, because the grand plan of God will apply to everyone. During the working of the details, there will be those who are drawn towards Him and those that will walk away from Him. It is important to note that He had compassion on anyone at any time who wanted to serve the God of Israel. That included foreigners in the land. There is a sense that God’s mercy always applies to those who seek after Him now, but will apply to everyone in the future when pain and misery is removed.

James 2:8-13: (NASB) 8If, however, you are fulfilling the royal law according to the Scripture, You shall love your neighbor as yourself, you are doing well. 9But if you show partiality, you are committing sin and are convicted by the law as transgressors. 10For whoever keeps the whole law and yet stumbles in one point, he has become guilty of all. 11For He who said, Do not commit adultery, also said, Do not commit murder. Now if you do not commit adultery, but do commit murder, you have become a transgressor of the law. 12So speak and so act as those who are to be judged by the law of liberty. 13For judgment will be merciless to one who has shown no mercy; mercy triumphs over judgment.

We are to be a conduit of mercy. God’s mercy flows into us, gets reworked as mercy to others and flows out from us. We have received magnificent mercy! We live under liberty which encourages mercy. We are obligated, therefore, to extend mercy. Do all these things and triumph over judgment! Mercy opens the door for grace.

Through God’s love, He created a world in which it would be justice-related. Mercy cannot properly and appropriately exist unless it is founded in justice. If you don’t have mercy, you can’t open the door to grace. Grace is granting you favor that is not deserved; mercy is taking away consequences that are deserved – pain and suffering as a result of what you did.

God’s love, justice, mercy and grace show us how we should build our lives based on love first. If we love one another in a just manner, we can figure out how to be merciful. We don’t have grace we can give others, but we can share God’s grace with them. That’s where mercy fits in our lives! It opens our lives to God’s grace.

James 1:22: (NIV) Do not merely listen to the word, and so deceive yourselves. Do what it says.

Don’t just listen to the word of God…do what it is says! Mercy is an action! We can think about mercy, dream about mercy, write about mercy and sing songs about mercy! But unless we do it, it is meaningless. Put mercy where it belongs so God’s grace can be opened up to those around us.

So what does it mean to be merciful?
