## Episode 1335 — What Is the Broad Road That Leads to Destruction? (Listener Q&A Series)
Published: 2024-05-28
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/doctrine/1335-broad-road/

What Is the Broad Road That Leads to Destruction?

Matthew 7:13–14: 13 Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. 14 For the gate is small and the way is narrow that leads to life, and there are few who find it.

Jesus plainly taught that the vast majority of humanity is traveling on the broad way that leads to destruction. Further, he taught there is a narrow way that leads to life, which is only found by few. For anyone who truly cares about humanity, this can be a very troubling thought. Why would God, the Creator of all things, set up a plan that has such a losing proposition? Was Jesus really saying that there are only a few who will ultimately be saved? If these things are true, then what about all those scriptures that say Jesus died for ALL? If this is not the true understanding, then what does this broad road to destruction actually refer to? Fortunately, this can all get sorted out by putting several pieces of biblical reasoning together.

When did the broad road to destruction begin?

1 Corinthians 15:22: For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.

Six thousand years ago, a sinner named Adam started on this road. Over 900 years later he died, and so has the whole human race who came from him. In Adam all die―there’s no disputing this. We are all on a road to being destroyed in death.

Adam was a perfect man, given the ability to think and choose:

Genesis 1:27–28: 27 God created man in His own image, in the image of God He created him; male and female He created them. 28 God blessed them; and God said to them, Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth, and subdue it; and rule over the fish of the sea and over the birds of the sky and over every living thing that moves on the earth.

Adam had everything going for him. He was given dominion over all the earth, he was blessed of God, he was created in God’s image, but he had loyalty choices to make to keep all of that.

Adam chose disobedience:

Genesis 3:6: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was desirable to make one wise, she took from its fruit and ate; and she gave also to her husband with her, and he ate.

We know from 2 Corinthians 11:3 that Eve was deceived. But Adam made a choice. He knew he was going against God’s edict.

His choice led to a life of sin ending in death:

Genesis 3:17–19: 17 Then to Adam He said, Because you have listened to the voice of your wife, and have eaten from the tree about which I commanded you, saying, You shall not eat from it; cursed is the ground because of you…

God is telling Adam the ground will no longer easily yield its increase to him. It will be in a different state which will require hard work to make it yield. This was a consequence of Adam’s choice. …in toil you will eat of it all the days of your life. 18 Both thorns and thistles it shall grow for you; and you will eat the plants of the field; 19 By the sweat of your face you will eat bread, till you return to the ground, because from it you were taken; for you are dust, and to dust you shall return.

There’s no more existence. No more life. Back to dust. This is the permanent cycle repeating over and over with every generation until eventually, conceivably, mankind destroys itself. We can see how that could unfold in this world relatively easily. The dying process started by Adam’s sin included a life now to be built within the confines of imperfection, which we all experience. This meant toil and failure on a regular basis. This is when the broad road to destruction began! It was here, dying thou shalt die, that the entrance to this road was opened. This road is the way to permanent death in Adam. All of Adam’s children inherit this terminal disease of sin that leads to death:

Romans 3:23: For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.

Here’s the problem:

Psalms 53:1–3: 1 The fool has said in his heart, There is no God, they are corrupt, and have committed abominable injustice; there is no one who does good. 2 God has looked down from heaven upon the sons of men to see if there is anyone who understands, who seeks after God. 3 Every one of them has turned aside; together they have become corrupt; there is no one who does good, not even one.

The broad road to destruction is a sad and crowded place! Between the Romans 3 and Psalms 53 scriptures above, we are in a bad situation – the broad road to destruction! Being on this road has brought sin, pain, suffering and death: As in Adam all die. Let’s focus on the second part of the scripture we already read:

1 Corinthians 15:22: For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive.

There’s a one-to-one relationship of Adam and Christ, but what does this mean? Are all of the ill effects of the broad road to destruction suddenly and miraculously wiped away? If we just believe in Christ, is it a free ticket to living forever in heaven? No. It is a nice idea, but it is flawed. There is a process involved or people would go back to their same habits and would begin sinning again. How can all be made alive? To start the process, Jesus paid the price for Adam’s sin and therefore for all sins.

The act of Jesus’ sacrifice is like a sign on the broad road to destruction that essentially says, “DETOUR: POTENTIAL EVERLASTING LIFE AHEAD.”

Hebrews 10:11–12: 11 Every priest stands daily ministering and offering time after time the same sacrifices, which can never take away sins; 12 but he (Jesus), having offered one sacrifice for sins for all time, SAT DOWN AT THE RIGHT HAND OF GOD.

In the bigger context, the Apostle Paul is comparing God’s future New Covenant with Israel’s old Law Covenant originally given to Moses. The priests in the Tabernacle, and later the Temple, had to make continual sacrifices for themselves and for the people in order to make amends (atone) for sin so they could continue in a relationship with God. Moses was their mediator to go between man and God.

Jesus offered one sacrifice for sins for all time―he sacrificed himself as a perfect man. This is a stark comparison. The sacrifices in the Temple were to cease because the single sacrifice of Jesus replaced the continual sacrifices under the Law. Because of his ransom payment, ALL will be called from their graves. This IS the detour. All of humanity is freely given entrance onto this NEW road to life. So, century after century, everyone is essentially born on this huge metaphorical road that earth’s billions travel on until they die. It’s important to note―there’s nothing we alone can do about it. It doesn’t matter how righteous we are or how many good things we do; we keep dying. But because of Jesus, there’s a way to get off this terrible path. Jesus himself explains:

John 5:28–29: 28 Do not marvel at this; for an hour is coming, in which all who are in the tombs will hear his voice, 29 and will come forth; those who did the good deeds to a resurrection of life, those who committed the evil deeds to a resurrection of judgment.

We start with the baseline that Jesus dying guaranteed a resurrection for ALL. (KJV): As in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive. Two equal sides. We can picture this as an old-fashioned scale of justice where two things of equal weight are put on each side to balance the scale.

Jesus, a perfect man, gave his life as a substitute for Adam, a perfect man.

Here is how it balances: Jesus died to take the place of Adam.

Here is the execution: As a reward for his faithfulness, God resurrected Jesus to a position of glory. Jesus is then able to call each and every individual from the grave.

As each individual is resurrected, they are detoured off of the broad road to destruction― eternal death in Adam. By God’s grace, they are given entrance onto the road with the potential for eternal life.

Where does this resurrection happen? Mankind’s billions in their sinful state were never promised a heavenly reward when they die. Do they get resurrected in some sort of holding area?

No, it is all about earth. There are many prophecies in the Old Testament that talk about the kingdom on earth. Jesus says, Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven. It is an earthly picture, an earthly resurrection for this group. If faithful, those called to follow Jesus are given a heavenly resurrection.

Being given free entrance on this new road does NOT guarantee people will stay on it. There is effort required to walk in the ways of righteousness. Part of that effort is accountability.

First, there will be accountability for words spoken:

Matthew 12:36–37: 36 But I tell you that every careless word that people speak, they shall give an accounting for it in the day of judgment. 37 For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.

This is not a “free ticket.” It is not that every careless and cruel word we ever said is just washed away without worry. We will have to account for them and make them right. Second, there will be accountability for things done in this present life. The Apostle Paul explains:

Romans 2:5–6: 5 But because of your stubbornness and unrepentant heart you are storing up wrath for yourself in the day of wrath and revelation of the righteous judgment of God, 6 who will render to each person according to his deeds.

No one “gets away with” anything. What we reap, we will sow. There are consequences for the horrible things people have done. But they are not given in such a way as to beat people down. They are given in such a way as to build people up.

We come off the road to destruction only through the sacrifice of Jesus. Each individual will be raised from the dead and given an opportunity for life.

This road to destruction is our inherited birthright as human beings, but we are so fortunate that God IS love and has a plan that will change things!

Right from the start, God always had the riddle of sin and death figured out. Because of God’s plan being in place and active, we have already begun to see evidence of how things will change. Now we need to dig more deeply into that evidence. Let’s look into what steps take place when so that we can understand the final destiny of this broad road to destruction.

Throughout Romans 5, Paul focuses in great detail on the value of Jesus’ sacrifice. Let’s look at just one verse:

Romans 5:18: So then as through one transgression (Adam’s sin) there resulted condemnation to all men, even so through one act of righteousness (Jesus’ sacrifice) there resulted justification of life to all men.

There’s the picture of the equal scales again. This is just another way of saying, (KJV) As in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive. That one-for-one relationship we saw in 1 Corinthians 15:22 is also shown here in Romans. It’s simple! All of humanity is clearly included in being condemned to sin and death in Adam. Therefore, justification in Jesus (being free from the guilt of sin―specifically, Adamic sin) is applicable to all mankind as well. All mankind receives the negative consequences of Adam, but they also get the positive benefits of salvation from Jesus. It’s justice! The balanced scale is a good illustration.

While we commonly call these “scales,” they are technically called “balances.” A scale records the weight of an object by measuring the amount of gravity causing it to compress a spring inside. The same item will have different weights on different planets due to different gravitational forces. It will even change slightly on earth if you are on a very high mountain or at sea level. A balance measures the mass of an object through comparison between the things on the two sides of the balance. One side is of a known weight or mass. The mass of an item does not change no matter where you are in the universe, or whether you are on a high mountain or standing on the edge of an ocean, unlike weight. The illustration of a balance is especially poignant because the merit of Jesus’ sacrifice is constant all over the universe―it doesn’t fluctuate with the size of the planetary body you are standing on!

The broad road to destruction DOES have a detour; and that detour is for ALL:

1 Timothy 2:3–5: (KJV) 3 For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Savior; 4 who will have all men to be saved <4982>, and to come unto the knowledge <1922> of the truth.

Saved: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #4982 sōzō; to save, i.e. deliver or protect (literally or figuratively): heal, preserve, save (self), do well, be (make) whole

Knowledge: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #1922 epignōsis; recognition, i.e. (by implication) full discernment, acknowledgment Knowledge here means having full discernment―true understanding. That’s one way we know this is future―mankind definitely does not have “full discernment” now! And notice the order―all men are saved, made whole, and THEN come to this full understanding. 5 For there is one God, and one mediator <3316> between God and men, the man Christ Jesus; who gave himself a ransom for all, to be testified in due time.

Mediator: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3316 mesitēs; Thayer’s English-Greek Lexicon: 1) one who intervenes between two, either in order to make or restore peace and friendship, or form a compact, or for ratifying a covenant

2) a medium of communication, arbitrator A mediator is someone who sits between opposing parties. In business disputes, mediation is often used to negotiate to bring two sides to come to an agreement. Scripturally, Moses was a mediator between God and the Hebrews. These scriptures say it is God’s intention for all men to be saved AND to come to a knowledge of the truth. “Saving” comes before the disclosure of the understanding, and it comes about through the process of a mediator. While initially mankind seemed to be in a scary position because there are consequences for sin, now we can see there is a process in place to make this ultimately a successful endeavor.

Sinful humanity is invited to this mediation table because Jesus paid the price for Adam which resulted in their resurrection. All the pieces are in place for this to work for an eternal purpose and an eternal end.

With all of this in mind, how do we understand the second verse of our theme text?

Matthew 7:13–14: 13 Enter through the narrow gate; for the gate is wide and the way is broad that leads to destruction, and there are many who enter through it. 14 For the gate is small and the way is narrow that leads to life, and there are few who find it.

Again, humanity starts on the broad road to destruction. There is a detour off this road, made available when Jesus died for us all, allowing a resurrection―being saved out of death from Adam. Mankind is given time to acquire knowledge―full discernment―and Jesus mediates on mankind’s behalf to be able to reconcile back with God that which was lost in the Garden of Eden.

But now there is a “narrow way.” WHAT is this road all about, WHERE is this road, and WHO gets to go on it?

This is the narrow way of the followers of Jesus. If anyone would come after me, let him deny himself and take up his cross and follow me (Mathew 16:24-26 ESV). The New Testament has many scriptures describing a life of sacrifice. This is different from the detour for all mankind after their resurrection later on. This narrow way is a voluntary way of difficulty in the present life.

The King James Version describes it as strait―meaning narrowed by obstacles standing in the way. The way is narrow that leads to life―it is a hard road to navigate. We can see why those individuals who choose this road should be given something different because they are walking a much more difficult road. They are working to follow Jesus in this life, in the middle of all the mess of the present.

This is in perfect harmony with ALL being saved. At his first advent, Jesus called followers to become part of THE body of Christ―Jesus plus his faithful followers. The body of Christ plays a future role in closing down the “death road,” the broad road to destruction in eternal death.

The gospel clearly teaches two different categories of people benefit from Jesus’ sacrifice:

1 Timothy 4:10: For it is for this we labor and strive, because we have fixed our hope on the living God, who is the Savior of all men, especially of believers.

1. all men―all of humanity in one category

2. believers―Jesus’ followers in another category

1 John 2:1–2: 1 My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin. And if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.

An advocate is different than a mediator. An advocate is somebody who sits next to us and pleads on our behalf before a judge. A mediator sits between opposing parties.

We―John is writing to true Christians―have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous. 2 and he himself is the propitiation (satisfaction/atonement) for our sins; and not for ours only, but also for those of the whole world.

1. for those of the whole world―all of humanity in one category

2. for our sins―Jesus’ followers are in another category

This advocate relationship (1 John 2:1) describes those Jesus stands with and represents to God, versus those for whom he mediates in 1 Timothy 2:5.

Clearly there are two categories of people. The “called out” ones on the narrow way get Jesus as their advocate. The “everybody else” heading down that broad road to destruction get Jesus as their mediator.

Two different classes of people with positive effects from his sacrifice! Remember this scripture? Again, there are two different categories:

John 5:29: and will come forth; those who did the good deeds to a resurrection of life, those who committed the evil deeds to a resurrection of judgment.

1. resurrection of judgment―all of humanity in one category

2. resurrection of life―Jesus’ followers are in another category Judgment―God’s righteous judgment. We often confuse God’s judgment with humanity’s interpretation of judgment. The world is judged, but God’s judgment is righteous and far beyond our comprehension. It is kind and merciful. It is fair and just.

For example:

Acts 17:31: …He has fixed a day in which He will judge the world in righteousness through a man whom He has appointed, having furnished proof to all men by raising him from the dead. This is speaking of Jesus executing God’s judgment. This judgment will be just, but difficult. It will not be an easy road for those who were not true followers of Jesus. The world will have to suffer consequences and make recompense for their sins. But we are so fortunate that God will judge with both love and mercy.

His judgment brings harmony and righteousness for the benefit of all mankind.

Romans 6:23: For the wages of sin is death, but the free gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.

This is another reinforcement of, (KJV) As in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.

After everyone is raised in the kingdom, what happens to that broad road of destruction; that death road we have no ability to get off on our own?

1 Corinthians 15:20–26: 20 But now Christ has been raised from the dead, the first fruits of those who are asleep. 21 For since by a man (Adam) came death, by a man (Jesus) also came the resurrection of the dead.

Christ came, he was raised from the dead―and that changed the destiny of everyone. 22 For as in Adam all die, so also in Christ all will be made alive. 23 But each in his own order: Christ the first fruits (faithful disciples), after that those who are Christ’s at his coming (the general world of mankind), This shows the order of resurrection. 24 then comes the end, when he hands over the kingdom to the God and Father, when he has abolished all rule and all authority and power. 25 For he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet. 26 The last enemy that will be abolished is death. We have a clear understanding that humanity was headed into the pit of destruction for eternity. BUT… - because of the intervention of Jesus all those thousands of years ago, and - because of Jesus living a perfect human life which qualified as a ransom, or corresponding price, for Adam’s perfect human life, the destiny of humanity was changed.

Justice was satisfied!

Bringing the world back into harmony with God will be difficult. However, through difficulty will come peace, harmony and godliness:

Zephaniah 3:8–9: 8 Therefore wait for Me, declares the LORD, For the day when I rise up as a witness. Indeed, My decision is to gather nations, to assemble kingdoms, to pour out on them My indignation, all My burning anger; for all the earth will be devoured by the fire of My zeal.

Wait! The earth will be devoured by ﬁre―didn’t we say the “detour” after resurrection happens here on earth?

Yes! When we read prophecy, we have to put it into the correct context. All the earth will be devoured by the fire of My zeal seems like it would mean the earth is literally burned up. However, it is symbolic of the social order being burned up, destroyed. How do we know? Because of the next verse: 9 For then I will give to the peoples purified lips, that all of them may call on the name of the LORD, to serve Him shoulder to shoulder.

This is a crucial verse to understanding God’s future kingdom. For all that burning anger and devouring, it ends with purified lips, calling on God and serving Him. This isn’t an eternal fire picture with people being tortured despite not having full discernment, full knowledge. The whole of humanity is praising Him!

What happens to the broad road to destruction?

It is over because of the sacrifice of Jesus.

In fact, another road opens up!

Isaiah 35:8–10: 8 A highway will be there, a roadway, and it will be called the Highway of Holiness. The unclean will not travel on it, but it will be for him who walks that way, and fools will not wander on it. 9 No lion will be there, nor will any vicious beast go up on it; these will not be found there. But the redeemed will walk there, 10 and the ransomed of the LORD will return and come with joyful shouting to Zion, with everlasting joy upon their heads. They will find gladness and joy, and sorrow and sighing will flee away.

This is a beautiful earthly prophecy! We embrace the Scriptures to help us understand what happens to the broad road to destruction and what happens to all of humanity. While not without accountability, it is a good ending.

We started with the questions, What is the broad road that leads to destruction? Where does it lead? How does it apply to us? What do we have to worry about? But Jesus took care of this path. Each individual must play their part, whether they are part of that resurrection that goes to heaven with Jesus or part of the latter resurrection of judgment here on earth. There they will learn reconciliation through the righteous judgment of God. The broad road to destruction will be eternally closed!

So, what is the broad road that leads to destruction?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …

## Episode 700 — Is Slavery Acceptable to God?
Published: 2012-03-11
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/society/700-is-slavery-acceptable-to-god/

Proverbs 30:10: (NASB) Do not slander a slave to his master, or he will curse you and you will be found guilty.

We are fortunate to live in a country where the stated core belief is that all men are created equal. With such a basis, it is theoretically much easier to identify and condemn the domination of one over another against their will. Yet, slavery in many forms not only has existed for most all of history, it continues to exist in this age of enlightenment. The Bible is full of examples of slavery and full of God’s seeming acceptance of this practice. So, does God support the idea of slavery? Stay with us as we endeavor to unravel this very tricky and emotional topic!

Is slavery by God’s design?

Slavery is fashioned after the rule of Satan and not the rule of God!

Genesis 2:15-17: (NASB) 15Then the LORD God took the man and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate <5647> it and keep <8104> it. 16The LORD God commanded the man, saying, From any tree of the garden you may eat freely; 17but from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil you shall not eat, for in the day that you eat from it you will surely die. Cultivate: Strongs #5647, 1) to work, serve, 2) to labor, work, do work 1b1) to be worked, be tilled (of land) Keep: Strongs #8104, 1) to keep, guard, observe, give heed, 2) to keep, have charge of

Genesis 3:16-19: (NRSV) 16To the woman he said, I will greatly increase your pangs in childbearing; in pain you shall bring forth children, yet your desire shall be for your husband, and he shall rule over you. 17And to the man he said, Because you have listened to the voice of your wife, and have eaten of the tree about which I commanded you, 'You shall not eat of it,' cursed is the ground because of you; in toil <6093> you shall eat of it all the days of your life; 18thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you; and you shall eat the plants of the field. 19By the sweat of your face you shall eat bread until you return to the ground, for out of it you were taken; you are dust, and to dust you shall return.

Toil: Strongs #6093, pain, labour, hardship, sorrow, toil Problem of Child Slavery in Benine, Africa, CBS News

- According to Unicef, the overall numbers are staggering. 1.2 million children are trafficked each year worldwide, 50,000 of them in Benine alone. Many are sold by their parents. - Poverty fuels the slave trade, forcing parents to either sell their children to traffickers on purpose or inadvertently. - Traffickers often swoop on the poor remote villages, offering money for the children or promising paying jobs in bigger cities... God’s creation was equitable while Satan was a usurper, power hungry, proud and a liar. As a result of the of a choice to not obey God the Creator and instead obey Satan the usurper, the curse destabilized the “would be” (equitable) society. This sets up circumstances for slavery to thrive - the idea of domination of one person over another.

So, if slavery is not of God’s design, then why did he let his people have slaves?

Why wouldn't God just condemn slavery? Here are the guidelines to keep in mind as we look into the treatment of slaves and slavery within the ancient nation of Israel. All of the following laws were part of the blossoming culture of Israel. Many of these texts are general sweeping statements/principles that would obviously apply as background in the application of specific laws:

Exodus 21:16: (NASB) He who kidnaps a man, whether he sells him or he is found in his possession, shall surely be put to death.

This is a general application, very focused on the individual rights of each man.

Exodus 21:26-27: (NRSV) 26When a slaveowner strikes the eye of a male or female slave, destroying it, the owner shall let the slave go, a free person, to compensate for the eye. 27If the owner knocks out a tooth of a male or female slave, the slave shall be let go, a free person, to compensate for the tooth.

The Law inherently contained the warning against all abuse. Slaves were to go free if they were abused.

Leviticus 19:9-10: (NASB) 9Now when you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not reap to the very corners of your field, nor shall you gather the gleanings of your harvest. 10Nor shall you glean your vineyard, nor shall you gather the fallen fruit of your vineyard; you shall leave them for the needy and for the stranger. I am the LORD your God.

This was a blanket command of compassion upon the less fortunate.

Leviticus 19:33-34: (NASB) 33When a stranger resides with you in your land, you shall not do him wrong. 34The stranger who resides with you shall be to you as the native among you, and you shall love him as yourself, for you were aliens in the land of Egypt; I am the LORD your God.

There was to be a common respect for all men. God never advocated abuse of another. So when studying the topic of slavery in the Hebrew Law, we need to put it in context of the Scriptures we just discussed. 13 Colonies small part in the triangular slave trade, Choices Program - The 13 colonies were a relatively small proportion of the slave trade - in all about 500,000-600,000. (Source: McClintock and Strong’s Bible Cyclopedia) Again, a father might sell his young daughter to a Hebrew, with a view either of the latter’s marrying her himself or of his giving her to his son (verses 7-9). This does sound harsh, but we don't have a culture based on arranged marriages. Women simply did not have the same rights as the men. Why? Remember the curse on Eve? Your husband shall rule over you. If the young lady did not end up marrying him, she could be redeemed through the repayment of her dowry. This was not human trafficking. It provided for

her rights and human dignity. The servitude of the Old Testament was very different from the slavery in the world today. (Source: McClintock and Strong’s Bible Cyclopedia) In respect to marriage, there were some peculiarities which, to our ideas, would be regarded as hardships. A master might, for instance, give a wife to a Hebrew servant for the time of his servitude, the wife being in this case, it must be remarked, not only a slave, but a non-Hebrew. Should he leave when his term had expired, his wife and children would remain the absolute property of the master (Exodus 21:4, 5). The reason for this regulation is, evidently, that the children of a female heathen slave are mere slaves; they inherited the mother’s disqualification....

Exodus 21:20-21: (KJV) 20And if a man smite his servant, or his maid, with a rod, and he die under his hand; he shall be surely punished. 21Notwithstanding, if he continue a day or two, he shall not be punished: for he is his money.

The proper use of a rod was moving back into order. The rod was used as a method of discipline, it was not to be abused. The master could not come to the servant with a sword, an implement of war. The rod was to discipline, not to be cruel. (Source: Matthew Poole, Biblical Commentator) "With a rod" - a fit and usual instrument for correction, whereby it is implied, that if he killed him with a sword, or any such weapon, he was to die for it. "Under his hand" - i.e. whilst the master is correcting him. He shall be surely punished; not with death, for then it would have been said so, as it is before and after; but as the magistrate or judge shall think fit, according to the diversity of circumstances; and therefore no particular punishment is set down.

Judgment: Strongs #2920 krisis (kree'-sis); decision (subjectively or objectively, for or against); by extension, a tribunal; by implication, justice (especially, divine law):

1) a separating, sundering, separation 1a) a trial, contest So, is this “judgment” a process of discovery just like in a trial and not a time of slamming the hammer of punishment down?

Isaiah 42:1-4: (NASB) 1Behold, My Servant, whom I uphold; My chosen one in whom My soul delights. ## Episode 802 — Where Do We Find Wisdom?
Published: 2014-02-23
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/802-where-do-we-find-wisdom/

Proverbs 9:1: (NASB) Wisdom has built her house; she has hewn out her seven pillars.

All you have to do is look around – what do you see? There is knowledge, there is technology, and there are people, places and things. We rush and we are impatient. We want what we want now.

We text, but we don’t talk. We type, but we don’t write. We have “friends,” but we don’t touch. We have families, but we are not familiar. We build our dreams around ourselves, but we are lonely.

Why is there such a massive and growing disconnect between our lives and our contentment? It is because we are not wise! We are smart, we are even savvy, but we are not wise and this is a problem! What happened to us?

WISDOM, noun 1a: accumulated philosophic or scientific learning; knowledge b: ability to discern inner qualities and relationships; insight c: good sense; judgment d: generally accepted belief Youth sees wisdom as boring, Vice Chancellor 2011, Macquarie University (Australia) - As far as young people are concerned, wisdom is the province of ghost whisperers, extraterrestrials like Mr. Spock the Vulcan from Star Trek, and wizened Kung Fu sages: “Your body is the arrow; your spirit is the bow, Grasshopper.” Wise people are not only seen as old, alien, and weird but also bookish, risk adverse and unemotional. No wonder young people ignore their pearls of wisdom.

Our perception of wisdom is that it is boring and not updated!

The Scriptures explain what happened to us:

Romans 1:18-23: (NASB) 18For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men who suppress the truth in unrighteousness, 19because that which is known about God is evident within them; for God made it evident to them. 20For since the creation of the world His invisible attributes, His eternal power and divine nature, have been clearly seen, being understood through what has been made, so that they are without excuse.

The human race had ample opportunity to know and understand the massive creative ability of God. The strength, order and complexity of all of creation are before the brightest minds of men and yet all they see is their own thinking and their own doing and take all the credit for their discoveries. 21For even though they knew God, they did not honor Him as God or give thanks, but they became futile in their speculations, and their foolish heart was darkened. 22Professing to be wise, they became fools, 23and exchanged the glory of the incorruptible God for an image in the form of corruptible man and of birds and four-footed animals and crawling creatures.

Man’s professions of wisdom have taken the sacred human creation in God’s image and reduced it to just another animal. In so doing, we have removed heavenly accountability and replaced it with an ever-changing subjective morality.

Romans 1:24-25: (NASB) 24Therefore God gave them over in the lusts of their hearts to impurity, so that their bodies would be dishonored among them. 25For they exchanged the truth of God for a lie, and worshiped and served the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.

With this earthborn and sin-laden brand of “wisdom,” the inevitable outcome is to serve self – to find the lowest common denominator of degradation and proclaim that everyone can be truly equal and important!

And so, here we are. We have arrived at a place of information, power, speed and greed. All this and no peace or wisdom among us! Where can we find wisdom, for when we find it peace will surely follow?

Wisdom is available – we just need to be open to its deepest source:

Proverbs 9:1-6: (NASB) 1Wisdom has built her house, she has hewn out her seven pillars; 2She has prepared her food, she has mixed her wine; She has also set her table; 3She has sent out her maidens, she calls from the tops of the heights of the city: 4Whoever is naive, let him turn in here! To him who lacks understanding she says, 5Come, eat of my food and drink of the wine I have mixed. 6Forsake your folly and live, and proceed in the way of understanding.

A “Rick” definition: Wisdom is experience, observation and knowledge applied through the lens of integrity, justice and mercy.

So, what are the “seven pillars” on which wisdom resides?

“It's not what you look at that matters, it's what you see.” - Henry David Thoreau Good news - bad news, Our Loss of Wisdom (TED Talk), Barry Schwartz - The good news is that you don’t need to be brilliant to be wise. The bad news is that without wisdom, brilliance isn’t enough. It’s as likely to get you and other people into trouble as anything else.

First, let’s look at a text that defines wisdom from above:

James 3:13-18: (NRSV) 13Who is wise and understanding among you? Show by your good life that your works are done with gentleness born of wisdom.

What we do reflects the wisdom that we apply.

It is interesting there are seven descriptions of the wisdom from above: 14But if you have bitter envy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not be boastful and false to the truth. 15Such wisdom does not come down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, and devilish. 16For where there is envy and selfish ambition, there will also be disorder and wickedness of every kind. 17But the wisdom from above is first 1) pure, then 2) peaceable,

3) gentle, 4) willing to yield, 5) full of mercy and good fruits, 6) without a trace of partiality 7) or hypocrisy. 18And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace for those who make peace.

Think about the source of the wisdom that you are applying! We hope it is coming from God’s word.

Now let’s look at a text that focuses on personal application of godly principles:

2 Peter 1:3-9: (NRSV) 3His divine power has given us everything needed for life and godliness, through the knowledge of Him who called us by His own glory and goodness. 4Thus He has given us, through these things, His precious and very great promises, so that through them you may escape from the corruption that is in the world because of lust, and may become participants of the divine nature.

By God’s divine power, we have been given everything we need for godliness as long as we apply ourselves.

Again, the contrast between what we run from and what we are to run towards is important – seven more to add to the list to gain wisdom: 5For this very reason, you must make every effort to support your faith with 1) goodness, and goodness with 2) knowledge, 6and knowledge with 3) self-control, and self-control with

4) endurance, and endurance with 5) godliness, 7and godliness with 6) mutual affection, and mutual affection with 7) love. 8For if these things are yours and are increasing among you, they keep you from being ineffective and unfruitful in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ. 9For anyone who lacks these things is nearsighted and blind, and is forgetful of the cleansing of past sins.

A caller suggests that a prerequisite of true wisdom is reverence to the Lord.

Each of these lists contains seven traits and seemingly puts them in a specific order. Because the James text directly relates these to God’s wisdom and Peter relates them to the application of spiritual knowledge, could we not look at them together as seven pillars of wisdom?

What godly How it is wisdom is:

applied: JAMES 3:17 2 PETER 1:5-7 Pure… …Goodness (virtue) Peaceable… …Knowledge Gentle… …Self-control Willing to yield… …Endurance Full of mercy and good fruits… …Godliness Without a trace of partiality… …Mutual affection Without a trace of hypocrisy… …Love

The Scripture says God’s wisdom is pure – can wisdom ever be impure?

Purity and virtue are the first on these lists for a reason.

Pure: Strongs #53 hagnos (hag-nos'); properly, clean, i.e. (figuratively) innocent, modest, perfect God’s wisdom cannot be anything but pure. If we are seeking the greatest wisdom available anywhere, it must be the purest wisdom and for that there is only one source.

The mission of Christianity is purification:

1 John 3:2-3: (NASB) 2Beloved, now we are children of God, and it has not appeared as yet what we will be. We know that when He appears, we will be like Him, because we will see Him just as He is. 3And everyone who has this hope fixed on Him purifies himself, just as He is pure.

Jesus was and is the perfect example of God’s wisdom applied!

Virtue: Strongs #703 arete (ar-et'-ay); manliness (valor), i.e. excellence (intrinsic or attributed) Virtue is “moral excellence,” meaning doing the right thing even when no one is looking and even when it costs you something. One cannot begin to grasp or even begin to recognize the pure wisdom from above without virtue or else this journey will be corrupted from the start.

Jesus was virtue personified:

Philippians 2:6-8: (ASV) 6who, existing in the form of God, counted not the being on an equality with God a thing to be grasped, 7but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men; 8and being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, becoming obedient even unto death, yea, the death of the cross.

Jesus gave everything he had for the mission he faced instead of his own good. This describes the beautiful relationship between Father and son before creation:

Proverbs 8:22-30: (NIV) 22The Lord brought me forth as the first of his works, before his deeds of old; 23I was formed long ages ago, at the very beginning, when the world came to be. 24When there were no watery depths, I was given birth, when there were no springs overflowing with water; 25before the mountains were settled in place, before the hills, I was given birth, 26before he made the world or its fields or any of the dust of the earth. 27I was there when he set the heavens in place, when he marked out the horizon on the face of the deep, 28when he established the clouds above and fixed securely the fountains of the deep, 29when he gave the sea its boundary so the waters would not overstep his command, and when he marked out the foundations of the earth. 30Then I was constantly at his side. I was filled with delight day after day, rejoicing always in his presence.

God’s wisdom is pure and applied through moral excellence or virtue. There is a very humble quality in this first pillar.

Rules and incentives can backfire, Our Loss of Wisdom (TED Talk), Barry Schwartz - Moral skill is chipped away by an overreliance on rules that deprives us of the opportunity to improvise and learn from our improvisations. And moral will is undermined by an incessant appeal to incentives that destroy our desire to do the right thing. And without intending it, by appealing to rules and incentives we are engaging on a war on wisdom.

With too many rules and incentives in place, we lose the ability to choose the right way because it is the right way. We dumb down our motivation and act because we can gain something from it. There is no wisdom in our decisions. “What we do for ourselves dies with us.

What we do for others and the world remains and is immortal.” - Albert Pine Now that we have a pure message received with moral excellence, the next pillar of wisdom is to recognize and comprehend the message: Godly wisdom is Peaceable: Strongs # 1516 …we apply it through Knowledge: Strongs #1108 God’s wisdom is peaceable in a very comprehensive sense, for His plan is a plan of peace.

Peaceable: Strongs #1516 1) relating to peace 2) peaceable, pacific, loving peace

3) bring peace with it, peaceful, salutary

Luke 2:10-14: (KJV) 10And the angel said unto them, Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people. 11For unto you is born this day in the city of David a Savior, which is Christ the Lord. 12And this shall be a sign unto you; ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger. 13And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying, 14Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.

Knowledge: Strongs #1108 gnosis (gno'-sis); knowing (the act), i.e. (by implication) knowledge A deep and abiding knowledge of God’s plan can be transformative – dig deep to know!

2 Timothy 3:14-17: (NRSV) 14But as for you, continue in what you have learned and firmly believed, knowing from whom you learned it, 15and how from childhood you have known the sacred writings that are able to instruct you for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus. 6All scripture is inspired by God and is useful for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness, 17so that everyone who belongs to God may be proficient, equipped for every good work.

Godly wisdom is Gentle: Strongs #1933 …we apply it through Self-control: Strongs #1466 Gentle: Strongs #1933 epieikes; appropriate, i.e. (by implication) mild:

1) seeming, suitable 2) equitable, fair, mild, gentle God’s wisdom is suitable and equitable, as its basis is justice and mercy.

Self-control: Strongs #1466 egkrateia (eng-krat'-i-ah); self-control (especially continence): self-control (the virtue of one who masters his desires and passions, especially his sensual appetites) Because godly wisdom is equitable and a long-term proposition, it only makes sense that our application of it must pass through the gates of self-control. To be a wise steward of God’s mysteries we must learn to focus only on the plan and not on our own agenda:

John 4:31-34: (NASB) 31Meanwhile the disciples were urging him, saying, Rabbi, eat. 32But he said to them, I have food to eat that you do not know about. 33So the disciples were saying to one another, no one brought him anything to eat, did he? 34Jesus said to them, my food is to do the will of Him who sent me and to accomplish His work.

The bread from heaven was a bigger priority for Jesus.

People often mistake a gentle and kind attitude for weakness. Wisdom understands this and applies the necessary self-control to rise above this miscalculation.

“A man remains ignorant because he loves ignorance, and chooses ignorant thoughts; a man becomes wise because he loves wisdom and chooses wise thoughts.”

- James Allen, Above Life's Turmoil

Talent and skill, Will Smith (actor) - The separation of talent and skill is one of the greatest misunderstood concepts for people who are trying to excel, who have dreams that want to do things. Talent you have naturally. Skill is only developed by hours and hours and hours of beating on your craft. I have never really viewed myself as particularly talented. Where I excel is a ridiculous, sickening work ethic. You know, while the other guy’s sleeping, I’m working. While the other guy’s eating, I’m working. There’s no easy way around it. No matter how talented you are, your talent is going to fail you if you’re not skilled.

Godly wisdom is willing to Yield: Strongs #2138 …we apply it through Endurance: Strongs #5281

Willing to yield: Strongs #2138 eupeithes (yoo-pi-thace'); good for persuasion, i.e. (intransitively) compliant 1) easily obeying, compliant

How can God’s wisdom possibly obey or be compliant when it is pure, focused on peace and gentleness? Shouldn’t everything have to comply with it? Godly wisdom has a curious combination of an ability to bend along the way where possible for the sake of learning, while it is still firmly focused on and not violating its vision.

1 Samuel 8:4-7: (NASB) 4Then all the elders of Israel gathered together and came to Samuel at Ramah; 5and they said to him, behold, you have grown old, and your sons do not walk in your ways. How does humanity’s appetite for experience play into the wisdom of God? Endurance: Strongs #5281 hupomone (hoop-om-on-ay'); cheerful (or hopeful) endurance, constancy: steadfastness, constancy, endurance Once we understand God’s wisdom bends for the sake of teaching, though it never denies its own purpose, we realize the world will look at this and revile us for worshipping a God who allows killing, evil and innocent people to suffer. 1 Peter 4:12-14: (NASB) 12Beloved, do not be surprised at the fiery ordeal among you, which comes upon you for your testing, as though some strange thing were happening to you; 13but to the degree that you share the sufferings of Christ, keep on rejoicing, so that also at the revelation of His glory you may rejoice with exultation. 14If you are reviled for the name of Christ, you are blessed, because the Spirit of glory and of God rests on you.

“The primary cause of unhappiness is never the situation, but your thoughts about it.” - Eckhart Tolle

Education scripts and mediocrity, Barry Schwartz, Our Loss of Wisdom - Scripted, lock-step curriculum…here’s an example from Chicago kindergartens: Reading and enjoying literature and words that begin with “B,” the bath. Godly wisdom is full of Mercy Strongs #1656 and good fruits: …We apply it through Godliness: Strongs #2150 Mercy: Strongs #1656 eleos (el'-eh-os); compassion (human or divine, especially active) God knows that his human creation has a voracious appetite for experience and in His wisdom He has provided for that appetite to be filled within the context of sin. 2 Samuel 12:10-13: (NASB) 10Now therefore, the sword shall never depart from your house, because you have despised Me and have taken the wife of Uriah the Hittite to be your wife. 11Thus says the LORD, behold, I will raise up evil against you from your own household; I will even take your wives before your eyes and give them to your companion, and he will lie with your wives in broad daylight. 12Indeed you did it secretly, but I will do this thing before all Israel, and under the sun. 13Then David said to Nathan, I have sinned against the LORD. Godliness: Strongs #2150 eusebeia (yoo-seb'-i-ah); piety

Romans 6:1-4: (NASB) 1What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin so that grace may increase? 2May it never be! Does God’s wisdom really have a place for everyone?

Godly wisdom is without a trace of Partiality: Strongs #87 …We apply it through Mutual Affection: Strongs #5360 Partiality: Strongs #87 adiakritos; 1) undistinguished, unintelligible

Psalms 72:17-19: (NASB) 17May his name endure forever; May his name increase as long as the sun shines; And let men bless themselves by him; Let all nations call him blessed. 18Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who alone works wonders. 19And blessed be His glorious name forever; And may the whole earth be filled with His glory. Galatians 3:26-29: (NASB) 26For you are all sons of God through faith in Christ Jesus. 27For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. 28There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus. 29And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s descendants, heirs according to promise. Godly wisdom is without a trace of Hypocrisy: Strongs #505 We apply it through Love: Strongs #26 Without Hypocrisy: Strongs #505 anupokritos (an-oo-pok'-ree-tos); unfeigned, undisguised, sincere This final pillar of wisdom brings us back to the first – the pillar of Purity. Love: Strongs #26 agape (ag-ah'-pay); love, i.e. affection or benevolence; specially (plural) a love-feast

We must grasp this sincere wisdom from above and be so taken by it that we will not hold back anything for selfish gain, but rather in benevolent love we will live our Christian calling.

Wisdom says when we do fall, we brush ourselves off and figure out how to avoid that same action in the future.

John 15:11–13,17: (NRSV) 11I have said these things to you so that my joy may be in you, and that your joy may be complete. 12This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. 13No one has greater love than this, to lay down one’s life for one’s friends...17I am giving you these commands so that you may love one another.

“Give without remembering and receive without forgetting.” - Ben Franklin Lessons from 40 films, Yoda from Star Wars, Reel Wisdom - Luke Skywalker: All right, I’ll give it a try. - Yoda: No. Try not. Do… or do not. There is no “try.”

If you want wisdom in your life, “do,” don’t just “try.” Godly wisdom is a transformative action so that we can put our life in order.

So, where do we find wisdom?

Jesus tells us that he spoke in parables in order to fulfill the prophecy in Isaiah. Jesus is saying that God talking to Isaiah was just a picture of God talking to Jesus. ## Episode 730 — Communicate Much?
Published: 2012-10-07
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/730-communicate-much/

Hebrews 13:16: (KJV) But to do good and to communicate forget not: for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.

After talking about complaining last week, it makes sense to look at the flip side – how to communicate - for good and positive reasons that is! What makes a great communicator? Is it charisma? Is it your words? Your message? What about body language? Where does passion fit? What made Jesus such a master at drawing people?

Does the Bible define communication the same way we do today?

What do we envision when we talk about communication? com·mu·ni·cate verb 1: share 2a: to convey knowledge of or information about: make known <communicate a story> 2b: to reveal by clear signs <his fear communicated itself to his friends> 3: to cause to pass from one to another <some diseases are easily communicated> Our culture has tweaked and developed the definition of communication to be a deep and penetrating life experience. We see communication as an art to be accomplished on both the giving and receiving sides of the issue.

Our six-year old not listening, Everybody Loves Raymond (television show) - (Raymond and Deborah in a classroom on how to communicate better with their children) Deborah: We have a six-year old daughter and she’s a great kid, but she’s having trouble listening and she is very stubborn lately. - Raymond: She’s just a kid. That’s a phase, right? - Teacher: Well, this is a perfect opportunity for you to try some ‘active listening!’ - Raymond: Thank you, we’ll try that. - Deborah: Active listening? I’m not familiar with that. - Teacher: It’s encouraging your child to communicate verbally without influencing her with your own preconceived notions or opinions. - Raymond: Got it. Here we go.

Let’s look at a good example of Biblical communication as the Apostle Paul teaches us.

The text begins its communication by stating the context of a Christian’s life:

Hebrews 10:21-25: (KJV) 21And having an high priest over the house of God; (Jesus) 22Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water. (It continues with the responsibility we have to ourselves) 23Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;) (And concludes with our communication responsibility to our brothers and sisters) 24And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: 25Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching.

The Apostle Paul was a great communicator, both oral and written. You can have the greatest message in the world, but if it can’t be communicated properly, it is just a bunch of words. We also are to stimulate the brotherhood to good things.

What lessons can we learn about communication for this next sound-byte? Airplane pilot with communication problems, trying to explain to passengers - Pilot: We are still sitting here; we still have the problem but the tower is speaking mainly Spanish and I’m speaking mainly English. My Spanish is not good enough to find out what the problem is and the English of the tower isn’t good enough to tell me where the problem exactly is. Um, so I can’t really tell you what the problem is. I asked Frankfort to send a second flight plan…but that did not help. So I have no idea what the problem is but I can assure you we are working on the problem and deferring to some whatever the problem here is, which is hard because we don’t know where the problem lies.

Observations so far:

- You need to understand the language being spoken. This applies to men and women trying to communicate as well!
- The relaying of an inconclusive message is always an inconclusive message.
- The desire to inform is not enough to accomplish the mission of informing.
- For a leader to come across as uninformed but sincere can be humorous, but it does NOT build confidence.

Matthew 5:37: Let your statement be, ‘Yes, Yes’ or No, no’ and anything beyond these is of evil.

Our communication should be as firm and positive as can be. How do we do that?

How Does the Bible describe communication?

Reflecting feelings, Everybody Loves Raymond (television show) Ray is roll playing with the teacher playing the part of his daughter, who does not want to go to her grandmother’s birthday party. Ray is trying to learn how to better communicate with his six-year old. - Teacher: Ray, if I say to you, “I hate when you make me do things,” perhaps you could acknowledge my feelings by saying something like, “You feel that you don’t have any control over our plans.” Understand? - Ray: That doesn’t sound like something I would say. - Teacher: Come on, let’s keep going. - Ray: (begrudgingly) Yeh, let’s. - Teacher: “All my friends are going to the park, but I have to go to some boring party?!” - Ray: You think that the party is going to be boring? - Teacher: That’s it, Ray. See, you are reflecting her feelings back. “It’s just a bunch of grownups sitting around an old house. I wanna be with my friends!” - Ray: Uh, but Grandma has that big bowl of coffee nips!

How do we get better with communication so we can really be effective? The Bible does not seem to talk about communicating in the way that we often refer to it - from the standpoint of understanding feelings – it does however, give a number of examples of communicating through co-laboring, and through common cause. The only words translated “communicate” in the Bible are along these lines.

These next words are all VERY similar but deal more with actions between us and not necessarily words. Communication scripturally is more that we are headed down a common path.

Communicate: Strongs #2841 koinoneo (koy-no-neh'-o); to share with others (objectively or subjectively)

Galatians 6:6: Let him that is taught in the word communicate <2841> unto him that teacheth in all good things.

Communicate: Strongs #2842 koinonia (koy-nohn-ee'-ah); partnership

Romans 15:26: For it hath pleased them of Macedonia and Achaia to make a certain contribution <2842> for the poor saints which are at Jerusalem.

Communicate: Strongs #2843: koinonikos (koy-no-nee-kos'); communicative, i.e. liberal Only use: 1 Timothy 6:18: That they do good, that they be rich in good works, ready to distribute, willing to communicate <2843>; (willing to be charitable, giving to others to support them in a common cause) All of these words carry the sense of participation in another’s life and not merely contributing input to it. They seem to imply an understanding – a sense of “being on the same page.”

A caller suggested that if you are not arrogant, you are not only more likely to be heard but to hear.

Let’s look at verbal communication in the 21st century as we investigate the Biblical as well: 1 and 2 of 5 dials, Body Language and Vocal Power Tips, Kathy McAfee

- I like to think there are five dials on your “vocal dashboard.” Dial 1: Tone - your pitch, high or low. We all have a range. Sometimes if you are a singer, you have a really big range but all of us have a range. Dial 2: Tempo – are you a fast talker or a slow talker? You can speed it up, you can slow it down. Particularly in presentations, you want to slow it down 20-25% versus your normal conversational speed. We do have some control over our vocal presentation, so this can help us communicate. Taking a Biblical approach to “communicating,” to being deeply engaged in one another’s life, we note that many of the Scriptures become easy to categorize:

John 13:14: (NASB) If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet.

Romans 14:1-6: (NASB) 1Now accept the one who is weak in faith, but not for the purpose of passing judgment on his opinions. 2One person has faith that he may eat all things, but he who is weak eats vegetables only. 3The one who eats is not to regard with contempt the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat is not to judge the one who eats, for God has accepted him. 4Who are you to judge the servant of another? We have a responsibility in making sure that we are doing the right kinds of things in the right kind of way and contributing to the lives of others.

Colossians 4:2-6: (NASB) 2Devote yourselves to prayer, keeping alert in it with an attitude of thanksgiving; 3praying at the same time for us as well, that God will open up to us a door for the word, so that we may speak forth the mystery of Christ, for which I have also been imprisoned; 4that I may make it clear in the way I ought to speak. 5Conduct yourselves with wisdom toward outsiders, making the most of the opportunity. 6Let your speech always be with grace, as though seasoned with salt, so that you will know how you should respond to each person.

3. Communicate with PURPOSE:

There are circumstances in life where our communication may fall on deaf ears. So what do we do? We still continue to communicate. Remember Stephen when he was getting stoned to death? He continued to communicate the goodness of God’s work and the vision he had seen. He continued to explain to them how high the calling of Christ was and how low their actions were. They stoned him anyway! But his communication was according to God’s will, so it was successful.

What are some other Biblically-based approaches to communication?

Finding peoples’ values, Dr. John Demartini, The Circle (Australian TV program)

- Everybody lives by a set of priorities, a set of values in their life. Whenever they are living by their highest priorities and values, they have more fulfillment. Whenever they communicate to other people in their highest values, there is greater communication. Sometimes we tend to project ourselves down on people, talk down to them, and project our expectations onto them. We have these “alternating monologues” instead of communicating what’s important to us to what is important to them.

Romans 12:9-13: (NASB) 9Let love be without hypocrisy. Galatians 6:1-5: (NASB) 1Brethren, even if anyone is caught in any trespass, you who are spiritual, restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness; each one looking to yourself, so that you too will not be tempted. 2Bear one another’s burdens, and thereby fulfill the law of Christ. 3For if anyone thinks he is something when he is nothing, he deceives himself. 4But each one must examine his own work, and then he will have reason for boasting in regard to himself alone, and not in regard to another. 5For each one will bear his own load.

We have to be humble enough to help one another pick up the weights of life. Humility is so important with communication.

Values are fingerprint specific, Dr. John Demartini, The Circle (Australian TV program) - Aren’t we all on the same page these days? Some are really dedicated to their education; some are more dedicated to their spiritual quest; some are into business or wealth or fitness. Whatever is highest on their list is their identity. They revolve their life around it. Honoring that and caring about that is the secret to communication and a great relationship.

Hebrews 10:23-25: (NASB) 23Let us hold fast the confession of our hope without wavering, for He who promised is faithful; 24and let us consider how to stimulate one another to love and good deeds, 25not forsaking our own assembling together, as is the habit of some, but encouraging one another; and all the more as you see the day drawing near.

To know your brother is the only way to truly communicate with him. When we appreciate the values of someone else, we are able to positively provoke them. If you don’t know what someone stands for, you may not be able to determine that you are poking them and not provoking them.

What about the power of words?

(This certainly means a challenge for the radio!)

Now, just because words are only 7% of our communication does not mean that they carry only 7% of the weight of communicating – a significant portion of our body language (55%) and tonality (38%) are built around our words! 3 of 5 dials, Body Language and Vocal Power Tips, Kathy McAfee

- So you have tone, tempo and now timber, which is the quality of your voice. Do you speak clear as a bell? When you say the word “important,” do you hear the “t” or not? Does your voice have texture? Do you have a radio voice? If you have a cold, there is texture. Sometimes you want to be clear as a bell, so that is the “timber” knob on your vocal dashboard. With our words, there are many parts – why and how are they spoken? What is spoken? When, where and to whom are they spoken?

James 3:2-12: (NASB) 2For we all stumble in many ways. This is an interesting parallel - the smallness of the tongue and the 7% of communication by words on the sticky note. The tongue is small but potent – for good or ill!

See how great a forest is set aflame by such a small fire! 6And the tongue is a fire, the very world of iniquity; the tongue is set among our members as that which defiles the entire body, and sets on fire the course of our life, and is set on fire by hell (gehenna). 7For every species of beasts and birds, of reptiles and creatures of the sea, is tamed and has been tamed by the human race. 8But no one can tame the tongue; it is a restless evil and full of deadly poison. 9With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse men, who have been made in the likeness of God; 10from the same mouth come both blessing and cursing. My brethren, these things ought not to be this way. 11Does a fountain send out from the same opening both fresh and bitter water? 12Can a fig tree, my brethren, produce olives, or a vine produce figs? Nor can salt water produce fresh.

Communication is: 55% body language, 38% tonality and 7% words.

Our life will often reveal its contradictions in the words that we speak. We can’t bless and curse men. 4 and 5 dials, Body Language and Vocal Power Tips, Kathy McAfee - Dial 4 – Volume – there are times I want to raise my voice and times I want to lower my voice. - Dial 5 – The Mute Button – silence can be very powerful!
